Bill (No. 19) to amend the Post Office Act (Hon Rodolphe Lemieux) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1-compensation for loss of
registered letters-
What do you mean by ' registered domestic article? '

I will give the House a few explanations regarding this Bill. Section 9, subsection K of the Post Office Act reads as follows, in regard to the powers of the Postmaster General:
prescribe and enforce such regulations as to letters directed to be registered, as to him

Beem necessary, in respect to the registration of letters and other matter passing by mail, as well between places in Canada as between Canada and the United Kingdom, or any British possession, or any foreign country, and to the charge to be made for the same, not exceeding five cents per each letter or article.
As every member of the House knows, it costs five cents, besides the usual postage of two cents, to register a letter. We have two classes of registered letters, the international and the domestic. Under the terms of the Postal Union Convention held at Rome in 1906, the Canadian Post Office Dep-partment agreed to become a party to the following provision:
In case of the loss of a registered article, and except in cases beyond control, the sender or at the request of the sender, the addressee is entitled to an indemnity of 50 francs.
All nations which adhere to the Postal Union are now responsible to the extent of 50 francs for each registered article which is lost, that is to say, the proven value of the article. What we do for international registered letters which are lost we intend to do for domestic registered letters that are lost.
This regulation for indemnity for the loss of registered letters has been adopted by Great Britain and the United States of America. The regulation of the English Post Office Department for compensation for the loss of registered inland correspondence reads as follows:
Subject to the rule stated below, the Postmaster General pays compensation voluntarily and as an act of grace for registered correspondence, including parcels. The fee payable over and above the postage is the ordinary registration fee for two pence, the limit of compensation being five pounds sterling. Compensation in respect of money of any kind (coin, orders, notes, cheques, stamps, Ac.) will only be given in those cases in which the money is inclosed in one of the registered letter envelopes sold by the post office and the packet is tendered for transmission by the registered letter post.
My hon. friend sees that in England they indemnify to the extent of £5. We intend to indemnify to the extent of $25, as is done in the United States' postal law. Let me read the text of the postal law dealing with this indemnity:
As a part of such system of registration he (the Postmaster General) may provide rules under which the sender or owners of first-class registered matter may be indemnified for loss thereof in the mails, the indemnity to be paid out of the postal revenues, but in no case to exceed $100 for any registered piece, or the actual value thereof when that is less than one hundred dollars, and for which no other compensation or reimbursement to the loser has been made; provided that the Post Office Department or its revenues shall not be liable for the loss of any other Mr. LEMIEUX.
mail matter on account of its having been registered.
And the United States regulations based thereon read:
Indemnity shall be paid for the value of the lost domestic first-class matter not to exceed $25 in any one case in accordance with the law and the regulations of the Post Office Department.
What we do to indemnify the sender or in respect of the addressee, as the case may be, of an international registered letter, we should at least do in the case of our own domestic letters, and we shall follow the regulations in that respect adopted by two of the most progressive countries, England and the United States. Let me now give to the House a few statistics of interest in connection with this matter. What would have been the liability of the department for the last two fiscal years if the powers I am now asking parliament for had been conferred on the Postmaster General? It would have been as follows:
1906- 7	$ 381 33
1907- 8	 2,184 78
That is the proven value of the letters lost because we would not pay the $25 for each letter lost. We would pay according to the proven value of the loss. If a letter lost contained only ten dollars, we would only pay that amount. In certain countries I believe, however, they pay up the amount fixed by statute. Last year (1907-8) we would have been called on to pay $2,184.72, but $1,621.22 of this amount was due to the fact that a postal car was wrecked and totally consumed by fire near Moorhead on November 14, 1908.
How much was claimed as having been lost?

The amount claimed is larger, but still it is remarkable how very little is claimed, if we take into consideration the vast amount of registered mail matter which passes through the mails. I

have not the figures, but they are not large and of course fictitious claims have been made on the department.
The amount which a letter contained up to $25 is paid in full, and above $25, only that sum is paid?

Yes. This has worked verv well in the United States and England, and really we have been a little backwards in this connection. We ought to have adopted that last year, but waited until we saw how it worked out in other countries.
Will the hon. minister give some idea of the amount to be set apart for this work?

We claim that under these regulations more care will be taken by the officials and the department to trace lost letters. In fact, it will be almost impossible to lose a registered letter. Of course a car or a steamer may be wrecked, but, taking the estimates of previous years, the amount will be very small. There will be more care taken and the department will make more money, because many more people will register their letters when they know the department is liable for each registered letter to the extent of $25.
Will there be any change in the form of receipt given for a registered letter? Will the amount the letter is said to contain he stated on the receipt?

Yes. At present we have only the five-cent stamp, which shows that a letter is registered and there is no declaration by the party that it contains money. In the future, under the regulations to be framed, the amount in the letter will have to be stated if it is feasible.
There is no provision in the Act for ascertaining the amount at the time of registration.
That will be part of the regulations. We need not amend the Act for that.

As a matter of practice, the Post Office official will not take any notice of the amount you are sending. Will there be a regulation by which the postmaster is bound to ascertain, at the time of registration, the amount being sent?
There will be under the new regulations.
I presume that this is not retroactive?
No.

Because, I have a very interesting case of loss in my own riding, and I have not been able to get any report that the matter has been properly investi-24}
gated, though I have drawn the attention of the department to it several times.
Has my attention been called to it in the House?
I do not know.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) will send me a note of it
I have done the note part of it; I have written several letters and have been assured that the matter would be investigated. It will be a very interesting case if investigated.
I would like to know the case.

I will give the Postmaster General the facts on another occasion. I would like to ask him also if he has considered the question of making compensation to the person who suffers loss-outside of this matter altogether-through the dishonesty of a government official? It seems to me that in such cases compensation should be made.

I am glad the hon. member has called attention to this matter, vv nenever an official of the post office appropriates money from the sender or from the addressee, the department, as a general rule, after full investigation makes good the amount. We have a special fund in the department for that very object. Of course, the instances in which w'e are called upon to make compensation are very few, but it does happen, perhaps two or three times in the course of a year, that dishonesty is practised in these matters by a government official. In that case, we make good the amount. The regulation under which this i3 done was passed several years ago by my predecessor, Sir William Mulock.
Is there a regulation, or does the minister intend to make a regulation, to provide for keeping the address of an individual who registers a letter?
Yes.
It is not usually enforced.

Under the new arrangement the department will be on the alert, as it will not wish to pay $25 for a lost registered letter. We intend to make the most stringent regulations for the protection of all the parties concerned. If there is not sufficient protection under the present regulations, we will have them framed in the proper way.

I am not sure that the Postmaster General understands my question. I asked if the address of the sender would be taken. I have never known the address of the sender of a registered letter to be asked for.

Yes, the postmaster is obliged to have the address of the sender as well as the addressee. An invoice is sent from office to office following each registered letter. It is very difficult to draw a registered letter from its appointed route because of this invoice system, but with the provision that is here proposed we shall take even more care.

I think the regulation a very good one. Personally I could never understand why there should not be compensation to the loser of a registered letter when a registration fee has been paid. Many cases of loss have been brought to my attention, and some of these I have brought before the department. I have learned that registering simply means keeping trace of a letter, but without compensation in case of loss. It seems to me that a registration ought to be an insurance as well.

As I understand it, if postmasters lose public money through the act of burglars, they have to bear the loss. I have known cases where postmasters have desired to give up the money order business in order to get out of the risk, the public money that they have in charge being, no doubt, an attraction to burglars.

If postmasters have taken the necessary precautions, for instance by keeping their postal notes, money, &c., in a safe approved by the department, and by using due diligence, the Post Office Department generally recoups them any loss they may sustain in the way referred to.

Is there to be any means of ascertaining whether the value is in the registered letter or not? Any one in business knows that sometimes a man will claim to have sent certain money by registered letter, but the receiver says that the money to the amount claimed was not enclosed.
Under the new regulation the sender will have to prove the amount before it is sent, because the department will be called upon to recoup him according to the proven value contained in the letter.

I understand that there is a provision by which a person desiring to transmit money to a foreign country may go to a postmaster, make his deposit of money and get a receipt therefor, and that money will be paid to a person named in a foreign country. But in case the money is not delivered, what provision is there for the depositor getting it back?
The regulations concerning registered letters, as well as ordinary letters, passing between two countries, are framed by what we call the Postal Union

Pardon me. I do not speak of a registered letter. But suppose Mr. SPROULE.
I deposit money with the postmaster to be paid to a certain person, say in Russia?
We have postal conventions with different countries by which we restrict our postal or money orders.
Suppose I send $25 in that way and it is not delivered in the foreign country, how do I get my money back?

If it is lost in Canada and the Post Office Department is proven responsible, Canada pays the money. If, on the other hand, the loss is proven against the foreign country, the foreign country pays the money.

Is there any limitation fixed? In the two cases I refer to, over a year has elapsed since the money was sent, and the party sending it seems to have no redress, although he has made application time and again. The only answer he gets is that inquiry is being made. Is there any limit to the time within which this is to be paid?
No, there is no prescription.

Is there any good reason why the sum should be limited to $25? It seems to me that if the whole people of Canada, through their government, undertake to perform a service for individuals and fail in the attempt and lose a sum of money, the whole people, through their government, ought to make good that loss to the individual. It may be considered advisable to limit the sum that the Postmaster General should undertake to convey from one part of the country to another; but if that sum is unlimited, if a man sends $100 through the government and it is lost, it seems to me that the government should sustain that loss and not the individual.

I think if we changed the law and made the government responsible for the whole amount in case of loss, the people of Canada, so long as the present Postmaster General presides over the department, would have unbounded confidence in the department, and would be willing to confidde a much larger sum than $25 to the department for delivery. Why should the people be obliged to send these large sums of money through banks or express companies instead of through the government?

I may mention in this connection that I have under consideration a plan of government insurance under which the Post Office Department will take charge of larger amounts, though that plan is not yet ripe for legislation. At present, large payments are sometimes made through the Post Office Department by banks and companies, showing the confidence they have in the service, and that confidence is justified by the very few losses that have occurred. Registered letters are so well traced that banks and large corporations are sending relatively large amounts of money through the Post Office Department. If we carried larger sums we would have to provide a special system of insurance, with a rate higher than the present rate of five cents. My officials are now studying very closely a plan in this direction and perhaps next year I may take the House into my confidence on that subject.

I need not remind the minister what came to his notice last year, of a very heavy loss that occurred between Lindsay and Dunsford. I think $500 disappeared mysteriously, and the loser could get no redress. I may also remind him of another case that the late member for Durham, Colonel Ward, brought frequently before the minister, where an officer of the department was proven to have received the money for the money order and never transmitted the money order. Is it the intention of the department to make this Bill retroactive, so that the loser in this case could get redress?
That will not come under this Bill. I recollect Colonel Ward's case, and I examined the papers very closely at the time. Has my hon. friend read the report on that case, issued by the department?
I have not read the report, but I have read all the evidence except the final report.

I have the evidence and at the close of last session I satisfied Col.
Ward that he should not press the matter further, because it was a special case. I need not say anything more about it.

I could not let that pass, because that is a reflection either on the gentleman who paid the money, or it is a reflection on Colonel Ward. There is no doubt that the postmaster took the money, that is well established.

I would not reflect at all either on Colonel Ward or on the postmaster. The best thing I can do is to send the report to my hon. friend, and he will see that the department is not at all liable in that case.
Does not the department keep a certain amount of money from the postmasters for the purpose of making up losses?

Yes, in case of possible dishonesty on _ the part of the officials there is a special fund in the department called a guarantee fund; and wherever an official has been dishonest, and a claim is made on the department, an investigation takes place, and the money is paid by order in council if the department is liable.
Is that not a species of insurance for the transmission of money? I may say that I think it is a criminal offence to send a letter purporting to contain money, that does not contain money.
Yes, but under the new regulations the evidence must be given and made clear to the officers in the department that there is money in the letter. That is how we intend to frame the regulations.
Is the clause confined to money only or does it cover articles of value ?

Yes, all registered articles.
On the question shall the Bill be reported.

Before the Bill is reported, I desire again to present the amendment which I offered last year to the Postmaster General and which I then understood would he considered by him providing the revenue of the country would per-, mit. We remember that last year a considerable reduction was made on drop letters in cities or larger places where letter carriers were employed. Formerly the postage on drop letters in cities where letter carriers were employed was two cents. By the legislation of last year that was reduced to one cent in this way. Section 58 of the Post Office Act reads as follows :
On letters not transmitted through the mails but posted and delivered at the same post office, commonly known as local or drop

letters, the rate shall be one cent per ounce weight which shall in all cases he prepaid by postage stamps affixed to such letters.
The clause, as originally enacted has also the following words :
Except that in cases where there is a delivery by letter carriers the rate shall he two cents per ounce which shall also be prepaid by postage stamps.
By the enactment of last session these words commencing with ' except' were expunged from clause 48 which practically made the postage on drop letters, whether in cities, towns, villages, or rural districts, one cent. To my mind this was a decided discrimination in favour of the cities as they enjoy the free delivery while in the rural districts there is no free delivery. It would only be fair that the rural districts should receive some compensation now that the revenue of the postal department has increased to such a very large amount. I intimated when the Bill was up last year that I desired to move an amendment to give effect to the proposition which I then made and make now to have the postage on drop letters in all places where letter carriers are not employed reduced from one cent to one half cent per ounce. The reduction would be fifty per cent in both cases. Fifty per cent of the postage was removed from drop letters in cities where letter carriers were employed, and I proposed then that we reduce the postage on drop letters in all other parts of the country to the same extent. There is no question but that this would be quite a boon to the people. Merchants throughout the country would no doubt use the post office to a much greater extent in sending out their bills, circulars, and other material appertaining to their business; in fact, I think the post office would derive a revenue at half a cent an ounce which would very largely recoup what would be lost by the reduction owing to the very much larger use that might be made of the mails. No doubt many others besides merchants in rural districts, such as doctors and others sending out accounts for like purposes would use the mails to a greater extent, and I think it only fair that the rural sections of the country should be considered along with the cities in this reduction of postage. I take no exception-I took no exception a year ago-to the reduction on drop letters in cities; in fact, I believe I expressed my approval of it: I thought it was quite right and proper as the revenue of the country could afford it. But, whilst that was the case I claimed in the interest of the rural districts, one county of which I represent myself, that we should be put on a par with the cities and be given a corresponding reduction in postage. Hence, I have prepared an amendment which I will offer to the Postmaster General, and if he has found the Mr. HENDERSON.
revenue has been sustained that no material loss has accrued owing to the reduction of postage in cities, I hope that he will take this amendment into his favourable consideration and grant to the rural districts the same favour and consideration that he has been gracious enough to extend to the cities. The amendment I propose will be in the form of clause 2 to the Bill now before us and will read thus:
Section 48 of the Post Office Act, chap. 66 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, as amended by chap. 53 of the statutes of 1908, is amended by adding thereto the words following: Except that in cases where there is no delivery by letter carriers the rate shall be one half cent per ounce to be prepaid by postage stamps.
The effect of the amendment, if adopted by the House, as I trust it will be, will be exactly as I have stated, that drop letters in all places outside of cities where letter carriers are not employed, will be subject only to half a cent postage instead of one cent as now. That will be the entire difference, and I ask that the minister will favourably consider this amendment. I would like very much to have it submitted to the House. If it is not received by the minister this year I hope it will be another time, but I do not desire to do anything that will prevent its adoption at any future time.
What are you going to do provided this amendment passes, with those localities where rural free mail delivery is established P

Free mail delivery is yet in its infancy, and consequently I do not know that it will really be a factor in connection with this matter. Free mail delivery will be in the country and could not affect letters that are posted to be delivered in any village or town by the citizens of that village or town. I beg to submit this amendment, moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Chisholm).

There are obvious reasons why I should express the hope that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) will not press his amendment. I do not receive the amendment in any bad spirit; on the contrary, it would possibly commend itself to me were I fully informed of the operation of the effect of reducing the drop letter rate in cities from two cents to one cent. It is quite true that last session I promised my hon. friend that if there were no loss in the revenue because of reducing the drop letter rate in cities I might perhaps extend the favour of the rural sections, but my hon. friend will remember that the promise was given not a year ago, but only a few months ago when the House was in session. From what statistics I have been able to gather I think it is fairly safe to assume

that the reduction of the drop letter rate will not eventually result in a loss of revenue, but we must at least wait for one fiscal year to pass before we can pronounce on that with certainty. When we have that information complete I will look forward with hope to the possibility of granting the boon to the rural sections proposed by the amendment of my hon. friend.

In view of the pro mise of the Postmaster General it is probable that with his assistance at the expiration of the fiscal year I will be better able to get this amendment adopted than were I to press it now In view of the argument advanced by the Postmaster General, I rather think it will be my wisest plan to accept his proposition, feeling assured that should we meet here at the expiration of the fiscal year I will have the assistance of the hon. gentleman to extend this boon to the rural districts as it has been extended to the cities. I may say that the Hansard will show that the promise of the Postmaster General was that he would make this applicable to the rural sections in one or two years, and as that promise was given only last July the Postmaster General cannot be held too strictly. I will accept the hon. minister's offer of material assistance, but I may tell him that next session he will not find me quite so pliable if he should raise any objections.
Amendment (Mr. Henderson) withdrawn.
Bill reported.
Might I ask the Postmaster General whether he has yet established a postal service in Gowganda and improved the service at Elk lake?

My hon. friend is just in time with his question. The hon. gentleman called on me the other day to ask for a post office at Gowganda and a service between Gowganda and the railway, and this morning we received word from Ontario, that objection would be taken to the grant or sale of any lot on which a building could be erected until at all events a few ! weeks hence. We have written the Hon. Mr. Cochrane this afternoon, asking him to consider our case before any other, as our desire is to serve the public. If my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) will nress his friends of the Ontario government we will do our best on our side.
On the motion for the third reading of the Bill.

Next sitting of the House. ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT.
Hon. SYDNEY FISHER (Minister of Agriculture) moved second reading of Bill (No. 18) to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
Does this Bill contemplate making any change in the law or is it merely to carry out the law as it is supposed to be at the present time?

It effects a change. In the revision of the statutes a certain clause was transposed from one section to the other with the result that the amount which was to be paid in compensation was increased over the amount fixed by the statute which was being revised. This is an Act to amend the Revised Statutes so as to place the figures as they were before the revision. We want to revert to the original law. The present law has been changed from the original law.
Was that done intentionally or unintentionally?
Unintentionally, by the revisers.

As I remember the original law, it provided that the government should pay for the loss of animals slaughter ed because affected by certain classes of contagious diseases, one of which was tuber culosis. I brought to the attention of the minister last year or the year before, a case in which a person applied for compensation but gould not get it. What is the law with regard to that? Is the government responsible for the loss of animals which are slaughtered because affected by tuberculosis, or is it not?

It is not. The law provides that the minister may cause to be slaughtered animals suffering from infectious or contagious diseases or suspected of being so infected, and that he may order a compensation to be paid to the owners of such animals.

If tuberculosis is included in the list of infectious or contagious diseases, one would naturally expect that the government would be responsible for some portion of the loss sustained by the ! owner of tuberculous animals slaughtered by order of the government.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1-compensation to owners of diseased animals.
How did this change occur? Was it through some transposition of language or through some omission?

Section 12 of the old Act provides that the Governor in Council may pay compensation for animals slaughtered under the provisions of the Act. Subsection 2 provides that the compensation, if any, shall be two-thirds of the value of the slaughtered animal. Section 4 fixes the maximum of value. In the revision of the

statute the same words and the same amounts are used, but the amount is applied to the compensation instead of the value. The consequence is that the compensation may be as high as the full value, which was not intended, and I am simply moving to restore the provision of the original Act.
I understand that since the revision of the statutes in 1906 until the present Bill has been introduced, the amount paid in respect of) slaughtered animals has been unlimited.
No, it has been limited.
I would like to ask if between the revision of the statutes and this date the minister has paid any greater amounts for cattle slaughtered than he did prior to 1906, under the old statute.

No, because we have been fixing the values on the basis of the old Act, acting as if the old Act was in force. We had the power to fix the full value, but we preferred to have the law made correct, and to act within its limitations rather than upon our own will.

Since the outbreak of the foot and mouth disease in the United States, the frontier ports, as I understand, have been guarded by certain officials of the government. Gananoque being one of these points where people are crossing daily, 1 understand that two men are patrolling there, and in addition a veterinary surgeon has been sent there from some distance. I have received the following letter:
We have a veterinary surgeon here named Dr. Joint. The Department of Agriculture has sent a man here at a great expense to inspect or look after the hoof and mouth disease He is a veterinary surgeon. Can you find out from the minister why this is necessary when we have a fully qualified man here to do this work at a much less expense, and as we are anxious to have a veterinary surgeon here we think it very unfair on the part of the Agricultural Department to side-track it. The farmers of our district are anxious to have a veterinary surgeon here, hut if there is anything that can help him to make a good fair living, this riding should be considered and not some outsider. Anything you can do will he appreciated by the farmers and the townsmen of Gananoque.
Yours truly,

I think that puts the case fairly. We have a qualified veterinary surgeon in Gananoque, and yet the minister sends one in from outside point. The one he sent has been there for some time although there was no crossing until a few days ago when the ice took. Why was not the local vet. called upon ? Where there is a local vet. at one of these points, no matter what his politics-and I do Mr. FISHER.
not know the politics of the one we have- he should have the patronage of the department. I hope the minister will recall the man he sent and instruct Dr. Joint to do the necessary work.

I did not know of this case at all. I have not the slightest idea who have been employed except that as much as posible we utilize our own permanent staff on this work of guarding the frontier. They were not sufficient to do all the work, especially in the earlier days when the disease was very acute, and when we were making special examinations inside Canada as well as outside. We have utilized our permanent staff as much as possible so as to avoid the expense of employing others. The exDense has been very great any way. Where we cannot use the men on our permanent staff, we have tried to utilize the men on the spot as much as possible. I shall make inquiry into the case, and if the complaint be well-founded, I shall see that the services of a qualified man on the spot are retained.
Is the embargo in connection with the foot and mouth disease removed or not?

It still exists and is strictly enforced although we have been able to relieve it, so far as horses are concerned. But we have not considered it safe to relieve the embargo in the case of cattle and other live stock. We are only enforcing the embargo against those states of the Union in which the disease has occurred. The New England States have not been infected, and therefore we have not imposed any embargo on the State of Maine which adjoins my hon. friend's province.
What about the state of Kentucky?

That state is a long way from our boundary and is not infected. We shut out any animal coming from any state infected and which is quarantined bv the American authorities. We also shut out any animals which passed through those states. For instance if any animal from Kentucky passes through New York or Philadelphia, which are infected, it would be debarred from coming into Canada. But the places we are specially guarding are the frontiers of contiguous states. Wherever New York, Pennsylvania, or Michigan, which I think are the only three states infected, which touch our boundaries, we guard the frontier. In the case of a New England State, we only guard our frontier to the extent of preventing the entry of any animals which may have to come through Pennsylvania or New York, even if they originally came from an uninfected state. I may say to my hon. friend from St. John that we were obliged to make some regulation about the ship-

ment of cattle from St. John to Europe. One of the great dangers was that if Canada were suspected of having the disease, the quarantine would be enforced against us on the other side and our trade in live animals cut off. The port of St. John does one of the largest export trades in winter of live cattle to Great Britain. I am not sure if there are not regular lines of steamers from Portland and Boston which touch at St. John on the way to Great Britain. The United States regulations permit animals from states not infected, to be shinned from Boston or Portland to Great Britain. We would not allow that in Canada, and therefore had to make a rule that ships from Boston or Portland containing American cattle should not be allowed to touch at St. John, even for the purpose of landing passengers. We did that in order to protect our stock yards and wharfs at St. John from any possible danger of infection, so that there would be no danger of our export of Canadian cattle from St. John to England being interfered with. Until there is a change in the American regulations, we would not be justified in relaxing our own. I was in Europe at the time the outbreak took place, and was fortunate enough to have in Rome, when I was there, a prominent member of the Department of Agriculture in England, and our chief veterinery, Dr. Rutherford. It was largely due to that fortunate circumstance that we were able to show just what we were doing and prove to the English authorities that there was no danger to their herds and flocks from any importation of Canadian cattle, and the result was that no restriction was placed on the landing of Canadian cattle in the mother country. Suspicion at first attached to Canada in the minds of the English people, because in the earlier reports of the outbreak of the disease in the United States, it was stated that the disease originated in Ontario and that animals sent from Ontario to Philadelphia were infected. We proved conclusively that if they were, they must have contracted the disease in American yards shown to have been infected, where they were unshipped, fed, and watered. When this was shown to the English authorities, Canada was relieved of all suspicion in their minds, and they did nothing to interfere with our trade.

I have heard drovers in Toronto say that it would be a good thing to prevent, by law, the export of our cattle in cases of that kind, especially such cattle as many of those that are shipped from Toronto to Buffalo.
I do not understand.

The cattle going from Toronto to Buffalo, of which I speak, are of a very inferior grade and sold at low prices for slaughter in Buffalo. Had the export been prohibited, there would have been
no mention of Canadian cattle being affected over there. Certainly, some day, Canada will be quarantined by another country by reason of such conditions as these.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. F. Maclean) mean to say that after the outbreak took place we should have prohibited the export of Canadian or that the export of cattle should be prohibited altogether?
When there was an outbreak.
Then, we would not have been saved the difficulty.

I am not quite clear about the answer which the minister gave with regard to horses. Has any embargo been placed on horses purchased in the State of Kentucky that may have to pass through Pennsylvania or New York in order to come into Canada? Are these horses debarred from Canada?
I think not.

Listening to the reply of the minister to the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) I could not but think of the price paid for certain animals that were found diseased at the port of Point Edward. By the Auditor General's Report of 1906, page D-10, it appears that Mr. J. T. Brethour, of Burford, Ont., received compensation for eighteen hogs amounting to $1,533, and Messrs. Douglas & Son, of Mitchell, received $932 for twelve hogs, slaughtered on account of disease. As I understood the minister he was trying to lead the hon. member for North Grey to believe that compensation paid for hogs in years gone by had not been in excess of the limit he was placing in this Act. I could not but feel that he was trying to cover up some of his own wrongdoing in years gone by, for he evidently made a serious blunder in this case.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) seems to have forgotten a very essential part of the transaction to which he refers. He ought to have remembered that this money was not paid under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, but was paid out of the exhibition vote for animals that had been sent for exhibition purposes. These animals were paid for at full value just as any other exhibits that may be lost or destroyed while in our charge are paid for.
Where does the minister get authority to take money set apart for exhibitions and pay it out in this manner?

I have the authority, because the whole matter is in connection with an exhibition. These hogs were sent for exhibition, as we might send a reaper

or a binder. If that reaper or binder were destroyed while in our charge, and with us responsible for the exhibit, we should be morally liable for the value. On different occasions we have paid for exhibits which we have been unable to return to the owners.

Then, there is no limit upon the amount of money the minister is privileged to pay under such circumstances. Why does not he place, even in this present Bill, a limit upon the amount that he may pay for animals that may have been sent out of Canada for exhibition, and that are found, while' outside the country, to be diseased ?
The payment for these animals has nothing to do with the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. They were dealt with as any other exhibit would have been dealt with.
The minister would lead the committee to believe thai the government were exhibiting these animals, whereas the owners of the animals were sending the exhibit as a commercial enterprise.
No.

I would direct the attention of the minister to the discussion of last year. It was shown! that when the matter was brought to the minister's attention, he wrote a letter over his own signature stating that he did not see how compensation could be allowed. But when political influence was brought to bear, he had to turn about and pay the enormous prices mentioned. I rather think the amendments to the law that are now before us are made because this matter was discussed in this House last session.

It has nothing to do with it, in any way, shape or form. The hon. member (Mr. Blain) may not know it. though I think he does-that Mr. Brethour, who was pc id this amount, is a well known conservative. No political influence was brought to bear on myself, or, so far as I know on any hon. member on this side of the House.
The hon. minister (Mr. Fisher) is now introducing politics into it-
Oh, oh.

Yes; this is an old story with the government-to get some liberal-conservative to unite their influence with that of the administration. I did not raise the point whether these gentlemen were liberals or conservative. I pointed out last year that the minister had paid for hogs $150 a piece in one case, $160 in another case, $65 in another case and $180 in another case, these hogs having been slaughtered because they were diseased. The correspondence in the case clearly showed that Mr. FISHER.
the government were not clear as to whether the hogs contracted the disease in quarantine or at the exhibition. The question whether the owners were liberal or conservative is not a matter in which the House is particularly interested.

I am glad the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) disclaims any political element in this question. I understood him to say that in the first place, I declined to pay the money, but that when political pull was exercised
I did.
I simply answer that the gentleman to whom the money was paid is a conservative, and, so far as I know, never supported this government or the party that supports this government.

He may have got some good Liberal to intercede for him. I understood the minister to say a short time ago that animals coming from Kentucky would not be quarantined at the border, though they might come through a state in which contagious diseases existed. But I understood him to say previously that this would really ensure them being quarantined.

I told my hon. friend that I thought there had been a relaxation in the case of horses. Speaking from memory, I think the Director General of the Veterinary Department told me that in regard to horses the disposition had been relaxed, and that they might come from any state now.

As I understand the original Act, the provisions in regard to compensation are the same for horses and for cattle, and that it is a matter of discretion whether compensation should be paid or not. I would like to ask the minister whether, in ease of horses killed for glanders, he knows of any case where compensation has been refused?
I do not.
I am told that it is the invariable practice of the department to grant compensation in cases of that kind.
It has been for some years back, but it was not so years ago.
Where cattle are slaughtered for tuberculosis, are there not many cases where compensation has been refused?
Yes.

Then I would like to ask the reason for the discrimination. Why pay the owner of a horse which is slaught-tered for disease and refuse to pay the owner of another animal which is slaughtered for another disease? If the principal is right in the one case, it appears to me it should be right in the other.

At first sight my hon. friend would appear to be right. But we have to deal with these diseases in a practical way. In certain classes of contagious diseases, such as glanders and hog cholera we think we are within measurable reach of stamping them out. With that object in view we wish to slaughter, not only animals which are diseased and immediately dangerous, but animals which are sure to incur infection, and thus prevent them from spreading the disease. In regard to glanders we are in a position to do that. A few years ago we determined to try and stamp it out, and I am glad to say that we are progressing reasonably towards that end. I do not mean to say that we are likely ever to be able to stamp out glanders absolutely, and that there may not be occasionally a few sporadic cases in Canada. I think we can do with regard to glanders what we have practically done in regard to hog cholera. The situation is different with regard to cattle suffering from tuberculosis. Tuberculosis is a disease not easily recognizable. While we have a sure test of the existence of the disease in an animal, it does not prove to be a sure test to show whether the disease is communicable to other animals. As a matter of diagnosis, it is practically impossible for a veterinary to say whether, when he finds by the test tuberculosis in an animal, the disease has so far progressed a to become communicable and dangerous. I have no hesitation in saying that there are a large number of cattle which have responded to the tuberculine test and have been shown to be infected by the disease, but which were not in the slightest degree dangerous, either to other animals or to the human species. There is no test by which we can tell which animals are dangerous and which are not. But so far as the glanders are concerned, the veterinary experts inform me that in case of any animal that responds to the mallein test, the disease is sure to be present and within a short time, to be dangerous both to other animals and to men. Under these circumstances we feel it is our duty to try to stamp out the disease of glanders, and for that purpose to pay compensation, where necessary, for animals slaughtered in the interest of the public at large. The disease of tuberculosis has not reached that stage, according to the expert testimony of veterinaries and physicians. Under these circumstances I never felt myself able to undertake towards bovine tuberculosis the same action that we have taken in regard to hog cholera, where we have succeeded so well. In regard to glanders we have made long steps towards stamping it out, and I hope that within a couple of years it will have practically disappeared. I appreciate the difficulty of making people understand the difference. I would be glad if we could devise
a system under which we could hope, even by expending a considerable sum of money, to stamp out bovine tuberculosis, but we have not yet been able to evolve any such system.

In view of this explanation I suggest to the minister whether it would not be practicable or advisable, in case of certain diseases, to remove the provision of the former Act and to make payment compulsory, leaving a discretionary power, as at present, in case of other diseases. For instance, in case of a disease where the object is to stamp it out, and where a certain amount of success has attended the effort, as in the case of glanders, to make payment compulsory, while in other diseases where the same progress has not been made in stamping them out to leave them to be dealt with in the discretion of the department.

Practically that is what we have done, only we have made the payment in the case of glanders and hog cholera compulsory by regulation and not by statute. The system is made uniform under the regulations which were passed according to the provisions of this statute.

My reasons for suggesting that is this: It has been suggested to me by farmers that if they knew for a certainty that they were going to get a certain amount of compensation for animals slaughtered it would be an object for them to discover disease and have an animal destroyed, whereas, under the present regulation, it being a matter of discretion with the department whether they shall be paid or not, they hide it and keep it from being discovered. It seems to me that it would assist in stamping out the disease if the payment were made compulsory, so that they would know that they would get compensation for slaughtered animals.

As a matter of fact, they do know. It is thoroughly advertised that, in cases of glanders and hog cholera, they do get compensation, and it is also thoroughly understood that in cases of tuberculosis they do not.

I do not know whether I understood the minister correctly or not, but if I did his statement was to the effect that the reason tuberculosis is not included amongst the contagious and infectious diseases with respect to which farmers get paid if they have to slaughter animals that are affected, was because a veterinary surgeon could not determine at any stage whether there was serious danger of the animal affecting others.
Hardly at any stage of the disease.

I hardly think that a veterinary surgeon would agree with the minister in the statement that they are unable to tell, when certain stages are reached whether an animal is dangerous to the surrounding herd. Take, for instance, an animal where emaciation is going on rapidly; accompanied with a cough ; I do not suppose that the minister contends that a veterinary surgeon would not say that the animal was dangerous to others around it. If there is some stage at which the veterinary does know as a matter of professional knowledge that ought to be a strong reason why animals so affected should be included in the list, and I do not think that a veterinary would agree with the minister's contention that they are not included in the list because the veterinary cannot tell when they have become dangerous.

My hon. friend is quite right. If I said that-I will not deny it positively, but I do not think I did-I did not in any way desire to convey the impression that there was not some stage of the disease when the veterinary could not diagnose it as dangerous. You could very well have a number of animals affected with tuberculosis in such an advanced stage that an ordinary diagnosis would be sufficient to determine the disease, and I have been considering and discussing with my veterinary authorities the advisability of treating such cases of tuberculosis in the same way as we do glanders or hog cholera. While I confess that I do think it might reduce the danger I can hardly hope by that means or any other means that have yet been devised or thought out to stamp out the disease in the same way that I think we will be able to stamp out hog cholera and glanders.
It might not be possible to stamp it out, but the danger from it might be minimized very much.

Do I understand the policy of my hon. friend's department to be of this character that if an individual has in his possession an animal which is necessarily dangerous both to other animals and to man, that animal is destroyed or may be destroyed and compensation results as a matter of course, but that if an individual has in his possession an animal which is not necessarily dangerous either to other animals or to man, which animal may be destroyed, the compensation is altogether discretionary?
No, we take it as a matter of course that if we order destruction we will pay compensation.
Always?

Always, whenever we order it, but we do not pay compensation Mr. FISHEE.
if an individual kills the animal himself and comes afterwards to us and asks for compensation.

That is a phase of the matter that I want to mention to the minister. As I understand by the Act and from what the minister has just said, the only cases, no matter what the disease may be, in which he pays compensation, are those cases in which the destruction of the animal is ordered by the minister. Of course, I can understand that there may be good reasons for it, but I have had actual cases come to my knowledge, several of them, some of which I have communicated to the department, in which there seems to be a good deal of hardship arising out of the fact that the animal was necessarily destroyed, but not destroyed through the agency of the government. The people in the country do not know the law, but they do know that certain diseases are exceptionally dangerous. They know, for instance, that hog cholera and glanders are two diseases that are exceptionally dangerous, and that they require almost immediate attention. They call in an experienced and qualified veterinary and he directs-very often they think that they have a lawful right to so direct- that the animal should be slaughtered. I do submit to the minister that in a case of that kind, where it can be established beyond a doubt, that the matter was done in perfect good faith then in all honesty the government should pay. What does the minister think of that? I would say to the minister that if he likes he can separate the classes of cases. He can say that in these exceptionally dangerous cases immediate action should be taken and that in the less dangerous cases the present procedure should apply. But, I do submit to the minister it is a hardship, when a qualified practitioner comes in and orders the destruction of an animal, that, because, forsooth, the remedy was taken at the earliest possible stage, the owner of the animal should not have compensation, whereas, if he had allowed the animal to linger and communicate the disease to probably many others of the herd, and spread it throughout the neighbourhood, there should be compensation. Why should not a certificate by a duly qualified veterinary, whether there has been any action by the department or not, entitle to compensation when he has acted of necessity in order to prevent the spread of the disease? I have had several cases of that kind, three or four that I can recall at the present time. I have brought them to the attention of the minister, and I have one before him now. I have not lost faith that we will be able to succeed in this case. I think the law might be very much improved in that regard.

My hon. friend, I am afraid, is an advocate, and perhaps he is

interested because of having these particular cases, but I will recall to his memory the fact that when we raised the proportion of the value of the animal to be paid in compensation some years ago we threshed that question out here, and I myself was fully convinced of the danger. I had my attention very strongly drawn to the danger of exaggerated compensation. I remember my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) pointing out and urging upon me the danger of collusion between practitioners and the owners of animals. It was suggested that the fact that the owners were the clients of the practitioners would dispose the latter to perhaps slaughter a little bit hurriedly and value a little high. In the interests of the public treasury we have to guard against anything of that kind. While these diseases are dangerous, there is no great difficulty, if any, in a farmer isolating a case on his farm for a day or two until the government veterinary arrives. The law provides that any practitioner must notify the department at once when he finds in his ordinary practice a case of contagious disease, and we immediately order one of our permanent officers to go there and investigate. I venture to say there is hardly any part of Canada which one of the government veterinaries of wide experience, would not reach within a day of our receiving notice of the existence of the disease. There is a good deal in having experience in handling some of these diseases, because we find that a good many local practitioners who. are quite good veterinarians have never seen a case of glanders. I hope the district of my hon. friend is not so affected-
It is the finest county in the province.
Oh, no.

I venture to say that in the province of Ontario pretty nearly one-half the ordinary veterinary practitioners have never seen a case of glanders, and I say that with pride, and it is a source of great satisfaction to us. In the maritime provinces I do not believe there are half a dozen veterinary practitioners who ever saw a case of glanders. In some parts of the province of Quebec glanders was prevalent a few years ago and we had to spend a considerable amount of money and use a great deal of diligence to stamp it out; but we have succeeded and to-day there is not one case where there were ten a few years ago. I think in a short time we will be able to say that glanders is practically stamped out from the entire province of Ontario. I believe it would not be in the interest of the public treasury to depart from the rule, that where we pay compensation it shall only be done on the order of an officer of the department.

When cattle are sent in from the country to the abbatoir at Toronto and slaughtered, and then found to he affected with tuberculosis, both the buyer and the seller of these cattle are absolutely in ignorance of the existence of the disease until the animal is killed. The flesh of that animal is then condemned by the officer of the department under the Inspection of Foods Act, and as I understand no compensation is paid. Why should not compensation be paid for an animal condemned by an officer of the department after it was killed, as well as for an animal condemned by an officer of the department before it was killed? If compensation is paid in the one case why should it not be paid in the other? It is worthy of consideration as to whether compensation should not in such a case be paid to the person who suffers the loss.

The condemnation of an animal at the abbatoir as unfit for human food is entirely different from the condemnation of the live animal which is affected with a contagious disease. The principle of compensation under this Act is to prevent the spread of contagious disease among our live animals, while the condemnation of the carcass at the abbatoir is for the protection of the public health. The dead animal does not convey the disease to any other animal.
It conveys the disease to man if its flesh is consumed.

Yes, but that has nothing to do with the contagious disease spreading to other animals which the Act now under consideration is intended to prevent. When we order the slaughter of a live animal, we consider that the owner has suffered for the benefit of the owners of other herds and that in the public interest he ought to be compensated. As the animal is diseased and consequently not at its full value we only pay two-thirds of the value. _ The question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Porter) is an interesting one, and I dare say it will come up for discussion on the estimates for enforcing the Canned Foods Act.

While it is very important to prevent the spread of contagious diseases amongst animals, it is very much more important to prevent the communication of that disease to human beings, and in that light it seems to me that compensation should be granted in the case I have mentioned.	m

I wish to call attention to a provision of this Act which bears harshly on the farmers and horsemen of British Columbia, and which has been the cause of no little hardship in my own riding. I refer to the provision by which the government is nominally entitled to pay

compensation to the extent of two-thirds of the value of an animal slaughtered. The value of the animal is limited to $150 in the case of horses other than thoroughbred. A couple of years ago we had reports of the prevalence of glanders in British Columbia, in consequence of which government officials were sent into the various sections of the province with authority to apply the mallein test and to slaughter any horses which reacted to that test. In British Columbia a horse of the value of $150 is a very ordinary animal indeed; that amount does not represent one-half the value of the average working horse in that province. It certainly did not represent the value of a large proportion of the horses which were condemned under the mallein test and slaughtered, and for which their owners were only offered $100 in compensation. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to consider whether, in fairness to us in British Columbia who have to pay so much more for our horses and our cattle than the farmers in eastern Canada have to pay, there should, not be a provision in this Act stating specifically that this compensation should bear some relation to the real value of the animal, and if we should be so unfortunate as to again come under suspicion as we did a couple of years ago, that our farmers should not be so heavily mulcted as they were then. I know of case after case in which horses valued at between $300 and $400 were slaughtered, not because they had the glanders, but because there was a suspicion that they might develop glanders. They were slaughtered on suspicion only, and yet their owners received only $100 of compensation. The minister shakes his head, but I am speaking, not from hearsay, but of my personal knowledge of events that occurred in the city of New Westminster. The thing became such a scandal, the subject of such an outcry, that a meeting of horse owners was held, and a delegation was sent to the Minister of Inland Revenue, when he was on a visit to Victoria, with the result that the work of testing and inspecting horses was stopped, and from that day we heard nothing more about glanders in my riding. V hat I want to point out is that when dealing with British Columbia, in the matter of salaries, for instance, we make a difference as compared with other parts of the Dominion, and in most lines of business it is recognized that prices are higher in British Columbia than in other provinces. Therefore I contend that it is a hardship upon our people that this Act should continue as it is, particularly in the case of horses slaughtered, not because they have the disease, but because the mallein test seems to show a disposition on their part to contract it and that they might in time become dangerous to the community. The Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
owners of these horses should receive fair compensation, instead of being put to the serious loss to which so many have been put by the application of that test.

My hon. friend himself has shown that his statement of the case is not a fair one. I understand him to say that these horses did react to the mallein test. That being the case they had the disease, though it may not have been apparent in the animals' noses. The horses having once contracted the disease, the veterinarians tell us that it is liable to become bad at any time and without warning, so as to be communicable to other animals. In regard to the value of the horses and the payment of compensation, no doubt certain classes of horses in the west-in Saskatchewan and Alberta as well as in British Columbia-are a little higher in value than in Ontario or Quebec, although I do not think there is a very great difference. But it would be very difficult indeed to put in the Act a provision that in British Columbia the value should be allowed to go to say $100 higher than in Ontario, and that therefore the compensation should be somewhat higher. That would be a difficult thing to work out, and I am afraid that it would lead to demands in all parts of the country for discrimination. I would not like ,off-hand to agree with it, although I sympathize to a certain extent with my hon. friend's suggestion.

I would like to enter a protest against so light and airy a disposition as the minister has shown, in saying that I admitted that the horses had the disease because they reacted to the mallein test. I am not a veterinary surgeon, but I have sufficient acquaintance with the procedure in these cases to know that the department realizes that reaction to the mallein test is not a positive proof of glanders. So much is that the case that the department provides for no less than three tests at long periods apart. Though a horse may react to the test to-day, the veterinary surgeon does not say that it has glanders. He says: it may have glanders, and I will test it again. After a long time he applies the second test, and again says: I am not sure that the horse has glanders; I will test it the third time. All this is contingent on the owner of the horse paying the cost of quarantining it during the period it is under test, and also agreeing to absolve the department from all liability of payment of compensation if, on the last of this series of tests, the horse is found really to have glanders. If reaction to the mallein test were positive proof that a horse had glanders, the department would not make provision for a series of tests of this nature. I rise to make this explanation merely because I do not think it is a proper answer

to ridicule my presentation of the case, and to say that I admitted that the horses had glanders. I said that a great majority of the horses were condemned on suspicion only There are horses in British Columbia to-day which reacted to the mallein test, but their owners would not allow them to be shot, and these horses to-day show no suspicion of glanders.

My hon. friend is quite right in saying that under certain circumstances the department has agreed to the position he states. The rule of the veterinarians is that reaction to the mallein test is conclusive evidence of the disease My hon. friend says that some of these animals reacted once, and afterwards did not react, and were released. I think that possibly a few cases of that kind have occurred but very few indeed. We throw the onus on the owner because absolute quarantine is only granted as a rule where the owner has a very valuable horse and prefers to take the risk of not getting compensation rather than allow it to be slaughtered. He prefers to go to the expense of an absolute quarantine than have the animal slaughtered. All the veterinary authorities consider the mallein test as an absolute one, like the tuberculine or any other. That tuberculine test is practically absolute, yet cattle have been condemned and slaughtered, in which afterwards on examination no trace of tuberculosis was found. But the scientific world have taken the tuberculine test as being so absolutely sure that the number of cases in which it has not been accurate is almost infinitesimal. A similar experience may be found in connection with the mallein test, but that test is considered by the veterinary authorities as absolute.

I would ask the hon.
minister if he will take steps to ascertain whether it is not really the case that horses in British Columbia are so much more valuable than the average elsewhere, that he should make some discrimination in their favour.

I shall certainly look into the matter.
Mr.NANTEL. (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I notice, that under the law, the animal must be valuated by the minister or by a person appointed by him; and moreover, that the price to be paid must not exceed such figure, that is to say $150 for a grade horse and $300 for a thoroughbred.
It seems to me that the law could be made more simple, and thus prevent all the annoyances to which the minister is exposed. The way should be to pay an average and uniform price; two classes being made a certain price would be paid for a common
horse, and so much for a thoroughbred, the price being fixed by the statute itself. There would then be no necessity of sending valuators on the ground and by that a saving of many costs, and the minister would not be exposed to the annoyance nor to the accusations of undue favour given to political friends, as has been insinuated a moment ago.
Nevertheless supposing that we would not be very particular as to the price to be fixed, it seems to me that there would not be much inconvenience, because a horse affected with the glanders or other contagious disease has no value, and the owner must expect to lose. The above remarks apply with greater force to other animals.

It would be really more simple and easy for the minister to accept the suggestion of the honourable member ; but, unfortunately, I think this would give a sort of encouragement to owners of horses of no value; we would be paying too much for horses of no service and not enough for the good ones. We must encourage the betterment of the breed, and, I would rather pay a little more to obtain that end, even if it costs me more annoyance than to accept the way suggested by the. hon. member, which would undoubtedly be more simple, but also far worse.

ly he was given a clearance and allowed to sell his cattle or export them. His net loss on that transaction was between $1,800 and $2,000. True there was suspicion but there was no disease. Had the animals been slaughtered he could have received compensation; but I believe that under the circumstances he is not entitled by law to any. There should be some provision to meet cases of that kind. I can understand that very great 'care has to be exercised in inspecting cattle for export to Great Britain, but in cases where no disease actually exists the owner should be given compensation.

The case cited by my hon. friend appears to be one of hardship, and it is unfortunate that the owner had to suffer this loss. The details will be looked into and I shall be glad to know exactly the facts.

In the crusade against glanders some two or three years ago, can the minister tell us whether that crusade ceased because the disease of glanders was wiped out or whether it was because of the indignation excited among the ranchers of British Columbia partly through the inefficiency of the test and partly because of the inadequate compensation? I quite agree with my hon. friend from New Westminister (Mr. Taylor) that the compensation is entirely inadequate in the case of horses slaughtered in British Columbia, owing to the greater value of these animals in that province as compared with other provinces. It is quite possible to suppose a case in which a horse could be five times the value of the compensation paid. And for that reason, the difference of value should be put on it. I imagine the intention is to place a fair value on the man's animals. In our portion of British Columbia, far removed from New Westminster, an ordinary team is worth about $600-certainly, you could not purchase them for less than $500. And to put a price of the sort outlined by the government and pay_ two-thirds of it would cause a rather indignant feeling on the part of the farmers, especially if he thinks the test is not infallible and that sometimes his animals are slaughtered on suspicion only. I know that the feeling through the Okanagan and down the Similkameen was very strong, and I think that it was the cause of the action of the department being changed in the way it was.

I know that there was a good deal of excitement, but the department did not deliberately change what_ the hon. gentleman calls 'the crusade' in consequence of the protests made. We tried, as far as possible, to deal with the public in a conciliatory way, and to educate the public to an appreciation of an understanding of our motives and methods.

Speaking from memory entirely, I urged upon my officers to proceed with greater caution, and to, use-if I may say so-more conciliatory methods than they seemed to be exercising. As to change of policy, there is nothing of the kind; and that policy, I am glad to say, has practically brought about a cessation of the disease in British Columbia. I have no doubt that the condition to-day in regard to horses in British Columbia is enormously improved in consequence of what was done at that time. The difficulties in the way of making discrimination as to the value of animals in different parts of the country are very great, and I doubt very much if any such arrangement could be come to that would not work greatly to the detriment of the treasury, as well as bring about cases of injustice. I am willing to think about it, and see if anything of the kind can be worked out, but I confess that I cannot see any prospect of it.

I, for one, would object to an increase in the compensation for gland-ered horses. The reason is that a glandered horse is not worth a single dollar. I have had some experience as an inspector and I would certainly object to any increase in compensation for a horse proven by the post-mortem to have been diseased. A glandered horse is not only valueless, but he is a source of danger and may cost the country an immense sum of money. I remember one band of bronchos brought into the county in which I live, and the result of their coming was that disease was spread over the whole county. Therefore,
I object to pay over $100 for that which is not worth a ten cent piece, and is a source of danger to the country. Is it not a fact that the Canadian government is paying larger compensation for animals that are slaughtered in this way than any other country in the world ? And why should horses be worth more in British Columbia than in Manitoba? The city of Winnineg boasts, and justly, that it has the finest horses of any city in Canada. Why people in British Columbia should expect more for their glandered horses than people in other provinces, I cannot understand. Besides, such a thing would cause a great deal of dissatisfaction. This is the first time I have learned that the department is paying/ for horses that are destroyed on suspicion. Horses are not destroyed on suspicion. The very fact that the government allows the owner of the horse to reserve the animal to be subjected to the mallein test for the third time, I think, is a wise provision. I have tested horses for the third time and have found that they reacted, but the second and third time the reaction is not so marked as the first time. Besides, a horse whose entire system is permeated with disease might not react at all. That is one case where you have

to go by the clinical symptoms. So far as increase in the compensation is concerned, 1 certainly object to any.

I would point out that section 3 of this Act says:
-Section 82 of the said Act is amended by adding after the word 'disease' in the seventh line, the following words,-'or of the suspicion of such disease.'
If the hon. member for Proveneher (Mr Molloy) is going to be logical, he should move an amendment providing that no compensation be paid, for he is evidently under the impression that the government are wasting the people's money by giving compensation. But I feel sure he is astray on the facts, for, so far as British Columbia is concerned, there is at least a very strong feeling that animals have been slaughtered on suspicion, without knowledge.

I do not feel at all bound to move that compensation be done away with. I am proud that the Canadian people pay so large compensation as they do. But I honestly think that $100 for a horse that is not worth a dollar is enough. True, the owner suffers the misfortune of the loss of the horse, or even the loss of a part of his herd. A man not having enough horses to do his work may purchase a horse not knowing that he is introducing disease into his herd. I do not think the innocent buyer should suffer. But when the country helps to bear the loss to the extent it does, I do not think there is any reason for increasing the compensation.

It is astonishing how, in this world, circumstances alter cases and change the view we take of questions. I happen to be, not a veterinary surgeon, but a representative of western farmers. And I happen to have had a couple of horses destroyed by glanders. I found the compensation extremely useful as assisting me in contending with the conditions of a new country and the difficulties of the pioneer work in which I am engaged. From this point of view, I should be prepared to differ slightly from my hon. friend from Proveneher (Mr. Molloy). The western farmer must face circumstances of very great difficulty. He tackles a life which is entirely new to him; and when he has the misfortune to get a pair of glandered horses, I can assure you from personal experience the compensation comes in very handy. From the point of view of the country, it is not always a loss to pay that compensation, for there are homesteaders in the west who if thev had not that compensation in such a difficulty would be left for a considerable time without horses altogether, and the wealth that they would otherwise earn, not only for themselves, but for Canada, would be unearned. I think that, from that point of 25
view, even a broad and sympathetic view of the case of the settler would commend itself to my friend from Proveneher if he tried for a moment to forget that he is a veterinary surgeon and place himself in the position of the farmer. But from the public point of view, there is another argument to be urged. The man who knows that he is going to have the only horse which he has destroyed, with all the difficulties of his life to face, having to provide for his wife and family and needing something to tide him over the struggles that lie before him in the early years of his life as a settler, will be apt to hide for a long time the fact that his horses have the glanders. I think it is a wise policy to give every encouragement to the settler-up to a reasonable point, which, I think, is two-thirds of the value of the animal-to divulge at the earliest moment the fact that he has a glandered horse, and thus afford protection to the owners of animals with which the others might come in contact. On these grounds, both of sympathetic regard for the earlier settler in his struggles and of the public good, so far as that is concerned, I offer my hearty support to the attitude of the department and a modest demurrer to the view taken by the hon. member for Proveneher (Mr. Molloy).
Bill reported.
