GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of the Bill (No. 20) to amend the Government Railways Act.
What is it?

Last year, it will be remembered, the Government Railways Act was amended to change the conditions under which those suffering loss by having animals killed, could recover compensation. An error was made in not putting in the exceptions that are in the general Railway Act. I am advised by the Justice Department that the way to obviate the difficulty is practically to repeal what we did last year and introduce the exact terms of the ordinary Railway Act, and make it apply to government railways. It repeals what we did last year, and introduces a clause found in subsection 4, chap. 37, of the Railway Act, section 294.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

I do not quite understand how that will work out. It is intended that there should be a fiat granted, as in the ordinary procedure in the Exchequer Court? If not, how is it proposed that the Crown should be served?

It is expected that the department, in all these cases, will allow the privilege of going to the Exchequer Court, where we settle a great many cases. There has been a good deal of discussion, not so much over the court process of recovering, but over the fact that our conditions were not the same. The people suffering losses under the old Government Railway Act had to prove more than we propose to require of them under this new Act. This is in identical terms with the ordinary Railway Act, except that we put ' His Majesty' where the word 'company' occurs.

I am not criticising the object of the Act. It seems to me that the Crown when it engages in the business of transportation ought to be subject to the same liability for the negligence of its officers as any private corporation. But I wished to know how it is to be worked out, because this measure provides that compensation can be recovered in any court of competent jurisdiction. Now, as far as the Exchequer Court is concerned, we know that recovery can be had against the Crown there. There are rules of the court, and statutory provisions as well, providing that a petition should be presented. The Crown is not usually sued by its own writ; it is sued by a subject, by means of a petition, and a fiat on that petition. Then there is a procedure for service of a petition by depositing it in a certain department of the government. When you introduce a rough and ready provision like this, adapted, not to proceedings against the Crown but to proceedings by one subject against another, I was desirous of as-Mr. GRAHAM.
certaining in what way it will work out, according to the view of the government. I do not precisely understand that at the present time.	[DOT]
Last year it was thoroughly threshed out and section 29 was inserted amending the Government Railway Act by providing practically what we are providing here.
I am afraid my hon. friend does not understand me.
There has been no objection taken to the granting of a fiat in every instance in which it has been asked for.

I am not criticising the object of the Act; I am endeavouring to see whether or not it would be effective in its present form. If I am satisfied it will be effective in its present form I have no word to say, but I am not satisfied of that at the present time nor can I say that the assurance of my hon. friend absolutely removes my difficulty. It would be contrary to all precedent that the Crown should issue a writ against itself; therefore, you must proceed by petition, I presume, and yet this statute does not seem to make any provision for such a procedure. It says that the subject may recover in any court of competent jurisdiction. I am not aware that in any court other than the Exchequer court there is procedure at the present time, nor do I know there is authority in the judges of the respective courts to authorize any procedure for the purposes of a section like this. I may be entirely wrong in this, but at all events I would like to have some information on the subject.
Perhaps I misunderstood my hon. friend and did not catch the technical idea. This Bill does not provide in any way for the extension of jurisdiction to any court outside of the Exchequer court.
Then, it is badly worded.
Any court of competent jurisdiction means the Exchequer court in this case.
Where the Crown i3 a party that is the only court having jurisdiction.
That is the only court of competent jurisdiction.

Then I misunderstood the section. I thought it was the intention of the section to permit these proceedings to be had in the ordinary courts of the land and not confine them to the Exchequer court. Then may I ask why the draughtsman did not simply say: The Exchequer court? It would have re-

774 moved a great deal of misapprehension on my part to have done that. If the expression ' in any court of competent jurisdiction means, as the minister assures me it was intended to mean, the Exchequer court and the Exchequer court alone, it would seem to me to be a very much simpler mode of draughting simply to use that expression, and if it is intended to confine the remedy to the Exchequer court I would respectfully suggest that it would be better to say so.
There is no objection to saying that. We have just followed the language of the Act.

I think the difficulty has arisen from the fact that language applicable to suit between subject and subject has been applied to an entirely different thing, namely, to a petition by a subject against the Crown for compensation.
I would move that where we have the words ' in any court of competent jurisdiction ' we say in the Exchequer court.'

If it can be fairly worked out it would be very much better to give jurisdiction to the courts throughout the country rather than to confine it to the Exchequer court. However, that is a very large question and I would not be prepared to urge it upon the minister at this stage.

It is a question that I have been considering a good deal and possibly I may have something to say with regard to it before the session is over. In this Bill I am simply trying to remedy a mistake that we made last session.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Suppose jurisdiction were afterwards extended to the other courts would it not be well to leave the language as it stands in the Bill at the present time? It would save an amendment to this Act. By this Bill petitioners can only come to the Exchequer court and this would not have the effect of extending jurisdiction to other courts.

I am inclined to think that actions will be attempted in other courts under the language as it is at the present time, and they will probably fail. However, if the minister proposes to extend to other courts the jurisdiction to entertain proceedings against the Crown for compensation of this kind or otherwise I would not have any special objection to allowing the language to remain as it is at present for that purpose.

I would not like to commit myself at the present time. Possibly we had better leave this at it is and if such a change should be made later on it would not require an amendment here, as this would meet the case. This question ' 25i
is a large one; it means giving up a prerogative of the Crown which prevents any subject from suing the Crown except permission is granted to him. Therefore, to say that a person could sue the Crown; in any court of law would be to reverse the position which the Crown has always taken. I think it would be wise to leave this wording as it is at the present time as there is no other court that would have any jurisdiction except the Exchequer court.

If the matter is going to be considered and if this is going to have any general beneficial operation it would be necessary to give the parties the right to sue in local courts. It is not a suit for a large amount as a rule. It is an action for compensation for the loss of a few animals and unless the person injured can be given the right to sue in the local courts it is of very little advantage. If he has to come to the Exchequer court and prosecute his action he will not get much benefit. It may be that in that way the Crown frequently escapes but if the scope of the Act is extended in such a way as to apply to the courts generally, as it appears by the wording here, it will give the injured person a better opportunity to prosecute his claim. I might also call the minister's attention to the expression ' in any action ' after the words ' His Majesty '. That does not seem to read very well. I think it is intended to be ' by action in any court.' I would like the minister to consider whether it can be worked out so as to extend the right of action to local courts. I do not know whether it can be but it would be beneficial to parties having claims against the Crown.
The wording is from the Railway Act, chapter 37. We have followed it exactly.
It is bad wording.

My hon. friends should have got it right when they were putting it through. I was not here. This is whati we get for following a bad example. It is nothing new that we are introducing here to-night; this is to remedy something that was passed last session and we are endeavouring to get this tribunal a little closer to the people. The Exchequer court is a perambulating court and goes to the people instead of the people coming to it. If we should extend jurisdiction to the courts generally we would relinquish a prerogative that the Crown has retained from time immemorial. Whether that ought to be done or not is a question that requires consideration. There is quite a demand for it, I will admit, and we are considering it, but at the same time that is not proposed here and I would like to amend this Act so as to make it workable.
The principal element of an amendment of this kind is to do away with the necessity of getting a fiat for an action. *
Unless the Intercolonial Railway runs through the hon. gentleman's constituency this clause does not apply. I am trying to bring the government railway under the General Railway Act in this respect.
Would not the same law apply to the railways in Canada?
That which I am introducing now has been in the Railway Act for years, and I am simply applying it to the government railway.

I understand it has been held in the courts that if a railway runs through a man's farm and his cattle are killed the railway company is responsible, but if the cattle of a farmer through whose land the railway does not run are killed on the track the company is not responsible.

I am not amending the Railway Act at all; I am merely applying this provision to the Intercolonial Railway. Speaking from memory, I think it has been held that if a man's cattle get from his own farm to a place where they have no right to be and are killed, negligence may possibly be shown and he has not the same claim for damages as would the man whose cattle are killed having strayed directly from his farm to the railway.
I do not think that is right.

That is the general law and we are not amending it in any way.

I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to this Bill, and to ask him to have it stand. We are face to face now with the very big question of the protection of level crossings. ration of policy from him in reference to the whole question of railway crossings in Canada so far as they are governed by Dominion law. speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext: I see that my hon. friend appreciates the difficulty. I am not now going to discuss the danger of level crossings, nor the remedy that we may apply to remove the dangers as far as possible. We will discuss that a little later on.
The minister appreciates that I do not expect him to do so.

This question has attained so much importance of late that it cannot be delayed very much longer. I agree with every word uttered by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), and I am glad that the Minister of Railways expresses himself along the line we hoped he would. I have always felt that there was something in the,.vested rights of railways which were chartered before any provision in regard to the protection of crossings was made, and that they should be dealt with differently from railways that may be chartered in the future. But we cannot commence too soon to deal with the question, and whatever legislation is enacted for that purpose should apply to every charter which passes this parliament hereafter.

I agree a good deal with what the hon. gentlemen have just said, but I cannot for one moment concur in the idea that the Railway Act, the general law of this country in regard to railways, is not to apply to all railways. The spirit of the Act is that it applies to all railways to-day, and anything that may be passed by this House as a portion of the general Act should apply to railways already in existence as well as to new railways. That is the key-note of the Act, and I cannot agree with the idea that we are to have two laws on this subject, one for the new roads and* one for the old roads. But, certainly, the question must be settled this session, and on a broad, progressive basis.

It would not be exactly two laws. But there are two different conditions which we must recognize. The main idea is that we should try to attain the same objects in reference to both roads, but the machinery for the two may be a little different on account of the different conditions.

I think it ought to be done; and my main object to-night is simply to get this order in council and the schedule that accompanies it, put upon the record to give the minister an opportunity of saying whether we are to have a Bill this session dealing with this increase of capital, and whether that reference which was outlined by the then Minister of the Interior has ever been made, namely, that we were to have a reference to the courts to find out what thq actual cost of the investment of the Canadian Pacific Railway was. That is very important. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company to-day, I believe, claim that they are simply under that charter, and that the rates can only be interfered with by this parliament when their earnings exceed 10 per cent on the actual amount invested in the company. I ask the minister if it is so, whether that reference was ever made, and whether that amount has ever been ascertained. I also want to know whether he intends to introduce a special Act this session in reference to that matter, like that of seven years ago.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend definite information on this point. I do not know whether that reference was ever made to the courts or not. Perhaps I am wrong, but it strikes me that the Bill was necessary.
Well, why was it in the previous case?

If it is necessary, undoubtedly one will be introduced; but if it is not necessary, I am not in a position to state that it will. be. I think all the' conditions mentioned in that legislation are guarded in the order in council.
But the Minister of Justice held, not only that they should do it by order in council, but that it should be in an Act of parliament.

I am not arguing that point. If it is necessary to have an Act of parliament, no doubt there will be an Act of parliament in order to bring into active operation the order in council, or to confirm it I think the conditions in the order in council cover everything that is covered by the conditions in the legislation referred to. I think the company cannot issue stock at less than par. A great many people think, my hon. friend perhaps does not think, that one way to protect the public would be to allow no company to issue its stock above par, either. I am not expressing an opinion, but that is the opinion of a great many men with whom I have talked, who think that would protect the public perhaps more than anything else against over-capitalization, principally against what we call wildcat schemes. However, after reading what my hon. friend has said in the ' Hansard ' I will.be able to answer him more definitely.

Another thing. The power to control the capital stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway was in parliament in 1892, but for some reason or other it was transferred to the jurisdiction of the Governor General in Council, I would also like to know why there is this distinction between the Canadian Pacific Railway and other roads. If other roads wish to increase their capital stock they come to parliament and get a special Act, and" everybody has notice of that Act, and everybody can govern themselves accordingly. But the great Canadian Pacific Railway Company apparently can increase its capital stock by an order in council. Now when the road was first incorporated the control of its capital stock was altogether in the hands of parliament, but a strange thing has happened, and now the control of that road in regard to its stock, and it is the greatest road in the country, is a matter of order in council, and, as we saw in 1902, of an order in council that at that time was confirmed by an Act of parliament. I also wish the minister to look up that matter and be able to tell the people of this country how this change has taken place, and what there is to justify it.

In the matter of increasing the capital stock of a railway like this, I agree with the contention of my hon. friend from York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) that it ought to be a matter of legislation in parliament. I do not know what the provisions of the Act are, or whether it empowers the Governor in Council to do it or not. But if it does empower the Governor in Council to do it, it seems rather strange that the last time they increased the stock they did it by Act of parliament confirming an order in council. I would regard a railway corporation coming to this parliament
for consideration just the same as I would a company that wanted to extend their line, or wanted to extend the time, or wanted to amend their charter in some particular. When it comes before parliament asking for consideration, parliament, in its wisdom, should amend that Act in any direction that is absolutely needed in the interest of the people, and it is then for the corporation either to accept the Act with the provisions tacked on, or not ask for the Act. I do not think that parliament, in its wisdom, would go so far as to do any great injustice, but I do not think it would be doing injustice to a railway corporation, when they come to parliament asking for favours, if parliament should in its wisdom ask for favours in return on behalf of the people.

I would like to ask the minister what is the position of this matter. Has the government power to increase the capital by order in council, or is it necessary for the company to come to parliament with a Bill to increase the capital? The minister who passed this order in council must understand the situation.

I am not in a position to say whether it is necessary. I have been of the opinion that it was not necessary, but I cannot say absolutely. It is a question that has been raised at the moment and I would have to look into it.
Would the minister get the information and give it to the House at a later stage?
Yes. I promised the hon. member for South York to have his entire remarks investigated, or read carefully to-morrow, and give a reply to all the questions he raised.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Railways and Canals -Capital

Lachine Canals, to complete wharf and basins, $150,-
000.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: This is a revote; $300,000 was voted last year for this work.
Was there anything done under this vote?

Would it be out of place to ask the minister to give us some information with regard to the government's policy on the enlargement of the Welland canal or the building of the Georgian Bay canal? The country has watched these questions with a great deal of interest and I am sure that a great many members of the House would be pleased to hear what the government's policy is. The promise was made during the election that some day the Welland canal would be enlarged and the

people were led to expect that operations would be commenced in the near future. Others think that the implied promise was given that the Georgian Bay canal would be commenced soon. It would be very interesting to the country to know what the government's policy is.

I never made any promise that either of these works would be done immediately. I have expressed the opinion in this House and reiterated it in the country that the position that Canada holds this year in the grain trade would be more than maintained if we enlarged the Welland canal. Last year this House voted a certain sum of money to make surveys, and I will have to ask for the voting of another certain sum to complete these surveys. I have abiding faith in the power of the development of our waterways to cheapen our transportation, and I believe that it will not be many years when either one or both of these things will be done if Canada is to hold her place. But, at the present time, I am not in a position to state what the policy of the government is. The estimate and report of the Georgian Bay canal scheme are in the 'Department of Public Works, and they have been laid before parliament. The report of the engineers on the Welland canal cannot be brought down until the survey is completed, and that will take perhaps another year. We are going on steadily with the work, and I am asking for another appropriation to complete this. By that time I hope I will be able to give the House an estimate of what it would cost to complete the enlargement of the Welland canal, or to build it anew in part. My own opinion is that it would maintain the trade in the carrying of grain by water from the west to the east and do its share of carrying the package freight from the east to the west. Notwithstanding the fact that the State of New York has voted one hundred million dollars for the enlargement of the Erie canal, experts tell me that the Welland canal, if enlarged to take the larger class of vessels from Duluth and Fort William down to the end of lake navigation. Kingston, Brockville or Prescott, we can get a rate for the carriage of grain that will be less than any rate that can be obtained by way of the Erie canal.

I noticed during the elections remarks attributed to the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) to the effect that he had the assurance that if the government were returned to power again, thev would at an early date commence the enlargement of the Welland canal. I was somewhat curious to know what foundation in fact these remarks really had, and to that end I put the query to the Minister of Railways and Canals. But, I see that he rather fights shy of the question, and is not as desirous now of leaving the im-Mr. SPROULE.
pression on the country that it will be commenced at an early date as his candidate was when such a statement was going to get votes. I presume that something of the kind was carried on in the campaign along the proposed route of the Georgian Bay canal. I thought I saw some remarks by some of the candidates to the same effect, and I wondered then whether they had any inside information which justified them in making the statements that they did. I think it is well that we should be frank with the country, and it is equally correct that the ministers should be frank with us. I do not think that members of this House, when talking to the country, are justified in going beyond the information given to the House, because I do not think it is proper for the government to give any private information to any private member of parliament. I think the government should first give their policy to the country through the House. That is the duty of the ministers, and that is what is expected of them, and if it were the invariable practice there would be less credence given to such random statements as we see in the press from time to time when it is important to leave the impression upon the minds of the people that if a certain political party are returned to power wonderful things will be accomplished with regard to works in which they are interested. I do not see the hon. member for Welland in his place to-night; if he had been here I should have liked to have his explanation of it.
Would the minister kindly give us a fuller explanation with reference to the work that is proposed to complete in connection with the Lachine canal.
This is to construct the wharf and two basins on the north side of the canal to afford better facilities for shippers.
At what point?
At Cote St. Paul.
On the government's own property or on somebody else's?
On our own property.
Has this work been partially done already?
The work is just let and the only money expended to date has been for the purchase of cement. It was got by tender.
At what date was the contract signed?
Soma little time ago.
Who are the contractors?
The Canadian General Development Company. Five tenders were received.

As I understand it, this vote was given a year ago and this is simply a revote. Last year we were told the work had to be proceeded with at once and $300,000 was voted, and now we are told no work was done. Is it possible it was placed in the estimates last year to lead the people to think that $300,000 would be spent before the election? I suppose the tenders were called for about election time?
This work has nothing to do with the elections. If it were to have any influence on the elections I suppose we would have let the contract and had the men at work on it weeks before the election.
You could have promised it.	-
Promises don't go very far in this age. The session closed late last year and the money was not available until prorogation and the contract was not let until later.
Last year $300,000 was voted and this year you are asking a revote of $150,000, leading to the inference that $150,000 was spent last year.

Following the usual practice we took a vote for $300,000 last year, which was expected to complete the entire work. This year we expect we will only be able to spend $150,000 and hence we ask for that sum.

Your original intention was to spend $300,000 in one year, and now you have decided to spend $150,000 in each of two years.
. Mr. GRAHAM. If I followed my own inclination I would put in the original estimates the entire amount the work is expected to cost so that every one would know it, and that done I would take a vote for the money we expected to spend that year. In this case we have only spent a small amount for the purchase of cement and we are asking for $150,000, and next year we will ask for the additional $150,000.

That is exactly what I said you had done.
national works for the development of the country. Then, when the business interests of the country are prospering, it is time for the government to stay its hand in expenditure. I believe the government is seriously to blame for cutting down its expenditures in view of the depression which existed last year and which is pretty sure to exist this coming year. If work is actually necessary for the development of the country the money should be expended now.

The Lacliine canal referred to in this vote is in my constituency. The wharf accommodation is entirely insufficient for the immense traffic at that particular point; the basins are too small and accidents are continually happening there and at the Cote St. Paul bridge. There is therefore absolute necessity for additional wharf accommodation at that place and also for the enlargement of the basins. The work was projected a very long time ago and it is only now that it is being carried out.
The estimates state that this $150,000 is to complete wharf and basins, but as the minister says it will cost $300,000 altogether. Is it not misleading to use the words ' to complete?'
I think the word ' complete ' is out of place there.

It has always been the practice to show in one column of the estimates the amount of money voted the previous year and in another column to show the revote so that the House would know how much had been spent during the year. The changed form of these estimates is an innovation which leads to confusion and which gives a just ground for complaint. The present form in which the estimate is put tends to confuse the members of the House as to the amount of money expended and the amount needed to complete the work. A return to the old form is advisable. In addition, I would like to know who are the officers of this Canadian Improvement Company-the president, the secretary and the directors-and who are the sureties.

Is not the explanation that the order has been issued to economize during the coming year? At a stage in the history of the country when the ordinary business industries are more or less depressed the government is going to adopt the policy of cutting down the national expenditure in every department. I have always opposed such a policy on the part of the government, whether Liberal or Conservative. When the ordinary business industries of the country are depressed is the very time when the government should give the country the benefit of its credit and enter extensively into the construction of

It is an incorporated company. It is not possible for me at present to give that information, but I can ascertain who the members of the company are. These companies have to put up as a deposit a percentage on the contract. In this case there were five tenders and the lowest tender got the contract.

I would like also to ask the minister when it became the policy of the department to charge repairs to capital account. I notice that the second item here is to stop leaks. Is it the custom of the department to charge this to capital account?
These are leaks which have existed in the north bank for some time, very dangerous leaks. It is really a new concrete wall that we are putting up and it will close , up the bank.
Where did the government get the cement?
It was all purchased by tender.
I notice a separate item here for the testing of cement. Has that been customary? I thought that was done by regular salaried officials of the department.
We test the cement for our own works. These men are paid by the year to do this work, and this is the same item we had last year.
Will the minister tell us from whom he purchased the cement, the quantity purchased, and the rate per barrel?
This cement is all bought by tender. I may say that cement is cheaper now than we have ever had it before. This is bought from the Vulcan Company -in Montreal.
Does the Vulcan Company manufacture cement, or are they middlemen?
They manufacture.

There are two manufacturers of cement in that part of the island of Montreal that constitutes the riding of Laval: One is the Vulcan Portland Cement Company and the other is the Lakefield Portland Cement Company. They are situated about two miles apart.
Which company got the contract?
The Vulcan Company.
It is a Tory concern.
Is the Lakefield Company a Tory concern?
No, the Lakefield Company is a better concern for the government than the other company.
This cement is purchased by tender, and the contract is given to the lower tenderer without any variation.
How many barrels were bought from the Vulcan Company?
20,000 barrels at $1.62, f.o.b. at the works. I may say that the bags returned will make a reduction of forty cents a barrel.

I think the House will remember that a few years ago the government went into a speculation of buying * Mr. CURRIE.
cement in anticipation of contracts, and bought 30,000 barrels that turned out to be absolutely useless. I do not know what system the government had then or what system they have now of testing the cement, or whether this cement has been tested so thoroughly that there is no doubt about it. I do not understand why the government should buy cement in anticipation of the contract. Who were the inspectors?
One of our staff. We have a rigid inspection of our cement.
Has that cement been delivered?
It was delivered f. o. b. at the works.
Where is it now?
It is in our own sheds at Montreal, right near the works.
What is the next lowest tender?
I have not that information, but I can assure my hon. friend that the lowest tenderer got the work.

The point raised by my hon. friend from North Simeoe (Mr. Currie) is of sufficient importance to make it necessary to take a few moments to discuss it, and that is the point of charging these items to capital. Just consider the position we are in from a financial point of view. In the year 1908-9 we shall spend probably every dollar of our revenue on current expense, and every dollar that we add to capital account this year will be borrowed, say at three and a half per cent, on loans not due for fifty years yet to come. We are borrowing this money without making any provision for a sinking fund and are arranging that the third generation after us shall repay it. Is it just to them that we should charge ' stopping leaks in the La-chine canal ' to capital? Look over the list and you will see the same thing occurring everywhere repairing slopes and all that. Should these things be charged to capital?
Certainly,

And building wharfs ? We are building wharfs all through the maritime provinces and elsewhere and charging them to income, while here we are paying for a wharf from capital account. I submit that any money invested in capital account should be expended on something permanent, something that will stand for fifty years from now. It is not fair to put burdens on future generations if they are to have none of the advantages connected therewith. We ought to keep our public works in good repair, but we should do that without charging the expense to capital

account and borrowing the money to do it and making that money repayable fifty years from now.

I quite agree with the hon. member from St. Antoine that the leaks in the Lachine canal should be repaired. I am not an expert in that work, but we are manufacturing cement in the riding I have the honour to represent, and I do not see why the hon. member from St. Antoine should ask questions about these tenders, provided that, according to the judgment of the minister, the contracts were granted in the public interest. In a few days from now, perhaps a few hours, the government will be asked whether some repairs will be made to the wharf at Pointe aux Trembles; and I do not see any reason why those two factories in Laval county should not get the contracts for cement, provided their tenders be the lowest, or at any rate be judged by the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Railways as being the ones which should be accepted in the public interest. It is certainly absolutely necessary that those works on the Lachine canal, which are in a condition menacing ruin, should be repaired. That is my policy, and I hardly think that the hon. member from St. Antoine division will venture to criticise it.

This question is a very important one and might as well be tested at this point as at any other. I would move that the item to stop leaks on the north bank of the Lachine canal at Cote St. Paul be charged to income and not to capital.

My hon. friend is springing something new on the House. We are simply following in this matter the same practice which has prevailed for years both under his friends and ours. It is a practice which is perfectly defensible. The canals give no revenue, as a few years ago we made them free, and consequently there is no revenue account against which to charge these items. It is absolutely necessary to protect the walls and it is for that purpose we are asking that vote. Then I doubt if my hon. friend has any right to make the motion he did. This is a question involving expenditure. He could move to strike the item out or reduce it, but not to increase it or charge it against any other account. All he can do, if he does not approve of the item is to take the responsibility of moving that it be struck out. He cannot have it charged against income account by a vote. No member of the government could do that.

The question I have raised is one that can be just as well discussed and threshed out on some other item at some other time, so that I have no objection to withdrawing my amendment at this moment. But I shall bring the matter up again in the form of a resolution, so as to
put on record our opinion with regard to charging the repairs against capital account
I do not see why this item should be pressed when we do not know the amounts of the different tenders and who the tenderers really are.

I understand the minister to say that this cement was purchased by tender at $1.62 per barrel. I want to refer to what took place here the other night. I then asked:
How comes it that the honourable minister paid $2.50 per barrel for 85 barrels of cement bought from Kirby & Co., when he could buy that cement at Hull for $1.80.
To that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) replied:
That was but a small quantity and no tenders were called for.
I then said: You could purchase it by retail at $1.65. This item proves what I said the other evening. The Minister of Railways purchased this cement by tender at $1.62, but the Minister of Public Works went to some of his political friends and purchased 85 barrels at $2.50, showing fifty per cent profit.
From whom was the cement purchased?

The bulk of it came from Montreal. My hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) wants to know the particulars of this contract. I have already told him that it is a schedule contract. I can give him the details of the schedule if he wishes.

The hon. minister (Mr. Graham) must know that this is not an answer. Even though this is a schedule contract, he must know the quantities and he must have moneyed it all out or he would not know what vote to ask for. Now, a word with reference to the charge he makes that it has been the habit of his department from time immemorial to charge such expenditures as this to capital account. I take issue with the hon. gentleman and deny that the case is as he says. The money spent in repairs on the canals or in inspecting cement cannot fairly be charged to capital. And, as to the general question of our right to deal with this matter as proposed in the motion which has been withdrawn, we have not the right to move that an estimate should be increased, but we have the right to say whether an estimate should be charged to capital or to current account, and without the consent of the Governor in Council. Now, I understand that $150,000 has been expended and that $150,000 is a revote.

No, we had already discussed that before my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) came in. It is a little confus-

ing as it is presented. But, as I explained, we had a vote last year for $300,000; parliament sat until late in the season and we did not let this contract until December. Consequently only $40,000 out of the $300,000 has been spent. This year we expect to spend only $150,000.
. Mr. JOHN HAGGAET. If the hon. minister has entered into a contract, why does he ask for only $150,000? Suppose the contractor completes the work, will he vs ait for a year for his pay?
We expect that we will be able to spend only $150,000 this season.
What does the contract money out at ?

I gave all the information with regard to this matter when the item was before the committee last year. I did not suppose that these details would be required to-night, so I have not these details before me. But I have sent for them and will be able to give them soon.
When is the work to be finished under the contract?
At that time the minister will require the whole amount of the contract. Where will he get the money aftei the amount of this estimate has been spent?
From parliament, I hope; there will be a session in the meantime.

Does the hon. minister intend to follow the practice of the Department of Public Works and, at the end of the year, ask for fresh tenders for the uncompleted work, or is this contract for the whole work?

I hope that no person will be so silly as to take the objection which was taken against the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) in the last parliament. He proposed to extend a contract, but a member of the opposition strongly urged that he should ask for new tenders. The result was that it cost the country over $100,000 more than it would have cost. The contract in the case now betore us is for the completion of the work.

I strongly endorse the remarks of the hon. member for St. Antoine with reference to charging this amount to capital. If the department is charging repairs to capital, it ought to deduct 5 per cent annually to provide a fund for those repairs. I am rather sorry the motion was not pressed to charge this to current account.
This is practically not a work of repair, though it will have that

effect. The leak in this bank has been repaired from time to time out of current account, but now we are building a new concrete wall in front of the bank. I might say that it is practically a new bank.

The deputy minister has had time to figure out the total amount of the contract. I do not wish to do the figuring. There are officials in the department who are supposed to have this work finished, and the minister, of all others, is the man who ought to know the amounts before he lets the contract.
I know that my hon. friends opposite do not wish to be unreasonable. I have explained why I have not these details before me at the moment. I gave the details last year.
But that explanation was merely of an estimate, whereas now a contract has been made.

There is another anomaly here. The hon. member tells us that $40,000 has been expended under this contract for cement-the cement has been bought and paid for. And yet he asks also $2,500 for the purpose of testing this cement.
We are constantly buying cement for the repair of the canals, and we have to pay the salaries of the men who test that cement.
You don't mean to say that you charge to capital account testing cement for the purpose of repairing a lock?
The staff are charged to capital account. Just as the building of a cement wall is charged to capital, so testing the cement to build that wall is rightly charged to capital account.

But all the cement he requires for this work on the Lachine canal, except for repair of .the locks, has been bought already and paid for, and all the testing must apply to the material for repairing the lock and the wall; yet he charges that amount to capital account.
This cement is merely a bagatelle to all the cement we use on the St. Lawrence canals.
In case tenders were called for and the lowest tender was accepted last year, why does the government buy the cement? Why does not the contractor buy the cement?

We always supply the cement. As the ex-minister will agree, we want the very best quality of cement, and we test it. We make it a practice that our tenders shall never include the cost of cement; that we supply ourselves.

Is that the customary way of testing cement that goes into public works? I thought it was tested week by week and day by day, because sometimes you will get a consignment of cement a part of which may be very good and another part very poor.

We keep a staff of men constantly at work doing nothing else but testing cement. We test the cement as it is received, and also as it is used. We also test it for its keeping qualities where it is stored.

I understand you employ other men besides those employed in testing cement, and how is it that you charge a portion of the work to this vote and another portion to some other vote? What becomes of the contention of the minister that we cannot pay this out of revenue because it should come under capital account?	*

The whole work is in connection with capital account, and the expenditure ought to be charged, I think, to capital account.
Mr. SP'ROULE. For re-testing the cement?
We charge testing the cement to capital account.
But there are several employees who are paid by salary and who test cement regularly.
We have an engineer, Mr. Lordly, in charge of this work, and he is paid entirely out of capital account, whatever work he is engaged on.

There is another peculiar thing. You purchase $40,000 worth of cement a year before you commence to work. What were the peculiar circumstances that required the purchase of the cement at that particular time? In what month did you purchase it?
We want to have our cement ready so that the contractors cannot raise any question that we detain them. This cement was purchased recently, and the delivery was completed only a few days ago.
Perhaps the minister will tell us when it was paid for? Was it last year?
Part of it was, and the balance will be paid in this year.
When was the last payment made?
$32,400 was paid in January last past.
When were the tenders opened?
Very shortly after they were received. The tenders are marked by two officials and placed in a safe.
Can the minister tell us when they were received?
I cannot remember.
Was it before the elections?
They had nothing to do with the elections. But I can get that information.
I think the item ought to stand.
It was asked for in the usual way, and given to the lowest tenderer.
I cannot understand why he should purchase cement in the month of October for contracts to be performed in the following year.

The explanation given by my deputy is that the contractors expected to do some work this fall, and they kept urging us to get the cement. But they did not go on with their work until we had the cement a little ahead of time.
Did the minister say that the contract was let in January?

We were going to let the contract earlier than that. The contractors urged that we should be ready with the cement so that they would not be detaind. Contractors are always ready to find fault and to complain that they are being delayed. We preferred to get it ahead of time. The date of the contract was October 24.
Oh, oh.
That is the contract with the Canadian Development Company. That is not the contract for the cement. I have sent for the cement contract to give my hon. friend the date.
Let the item stand until it comes.
Did we understand the minister to say that he would ascertain the names of the officers of this development company which received the large contract?
Will the minister find out the name of the president of the Lake-field Portland Cement Company?
The contract with the Canadian General Development Company is signed by Beaudry Leman.

Surely the hon. gentleman would not enter into a contract with a company unless the contract was signed by the proper officers. I under-

stand it has to be under the seal of the company and signed by the secretary or the president. Surely my hon. friend has no right to enter into a contract without the signatures of those officers.
That would depend on the by-laws of the company. It is signed by the head of the company and bears the corporate seal of the company.
What is the name?
Beaudry Leman.
That is a well known name in the province of Quebec. He is an engineer. He is also a great nationalist, a friend of Mr. Bourassa.
I will send this contract over to my hon. friend opposite. There is the signature of the secretary that I cannot decipher.

I think we should have from the minister a list of the different tenderers showing the amount of each tender. There were five tenders and if we had that in detail it would go on Hansard. If the minister had come down and made the statement that last year there was $300,000 voted for this work, we have spent $40,000 of this amount for cement, tenders were called on such and such a date by public advertisement in the newspapers, and a contract was awarded on such a date to whatever firm got it, there would have been no trouble about it. I have been listening to ascertain what the position is and I cannot understand who the five tenderers were, what each tender amounted to or what the date of the calling for tenders for cement was. All we want is that little explanation and I for one undertake to say that the item will go through.

I have no objection at all to bring down the name of the tenderers. I do not think that my hon. friend as a business man will say that in connection with each of these items, unless the matter is questioned, we should give the tender of every man.
We are entitled to it.
The House has never asked for it but I will bring it over.
It has been the custom.

Where there has been any question as to the contract having been awarded to the lowest tender, of course, the tenders have been asked for. I will bring it over if my hon. friend wants it, but my experience in this House and in another House for ten years has been that unless there was a question as to the contract being given to the lowest tenderer these particulars have not been asked for owing to business reasons that any man will realize in a moment. But, if my hon. friend Mr. CURRIE.
wants it I will bring down all the tenders although business men do not like it.

The minister states that it has not been the custom in this House, but at any time we wanted any details with respect to any item the minister has always been able to supply them. We have the right to know the names of tenderers and in so far as I am concerned I want to know them now. The minister feels annoyed because I do want them.
No, I am not annoyed.

If the minister had a statement with regard to every item I am sure that the estimates would go through very easily. I do not think it is fair to ask us to pass these items in the way that the minister is doing to-night without offering to give us the slightest detail. The minister said that he gave all the details about this particular item last year, but I have been trying to find the details in ' Hansard '. They would be in ' Hansard ' if they had been given.
Not altogether.
There are a lot of men here now who were not here last" year.

I cannot find any thing at all in ' Hansard ' as far as this item is concerned. As my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) states, there are a great many new men in the House and they are entitled to the details which were given last year.
The original vote was $300,000, the minister has paid $40,000 for cement and he is spending $150,000. Does that include the $40,000 for cement?
No.
Then the minister has a large sum of money voted that will not be expended for two years. Yet, he has purchased all the cement and is going to keep it stored for two years.
This is not enough cement for the work.

Then there is a large quantity of cement bought and it is going to be stored until next summer to carry on this work. I again impress on the minister if this work is necessary he should expend every dollar of the money voted each year. The time for the government to stand to their guns and come to the relief of the people is when there is general depression in the business industries of the country. Men are out of employment all over Canada to-day, and the policy of the government is to throw more men on the streets and leave more mouths unfed by cutting down expenditure. If I had the power I would move to amend that vote.
I have not the power either.
The minister can take steps to get it done and I cannot.
Was the cement purchased by tender last year ?
Yes, we always purchase our cement by tender.
The Canadian Portland Cement Company sold you 5.000 barrels last vear at $2.62 a barrel; that is a higher price than you are paying this year?
Yes.
It is a dollar a barrel more. You also purchased 2,500 barrels at $2.40 a barrel from another cement company; were these contracts let bv tender?
All our cement contracts are let by tender and we take the lowest tender in every case. That price is gross, and we get 10 cents per bag for the four bags in each barrel, or 40 cents.

Portland cement should be supplied actually when it is needed as it depreciates greatly by keeping. The minister has purchased $40,000 worth of cement on a $300,000 contract and he will have to keep it a year or two before it is actually used.
We have just got delivery now and they will start using it on the 1st of April.
The half of that cement will be used this year and the rest of it in a year and a half, and if it is in bags it will be perfectly useless at the end of that time.
There won't be a bag of it left then.

The minister said this contract was entered into in January, but the contract is signed on the 24th of October. It will take me some time to figure out how the prices in the contract compare with the current prices and whether the contract has been really let to the lowest tenderer or not. I ask the minister to let the item stand so that we can have access to the contract in his department or somewhere else to-morrow.
In order to give my hon. friend the information he wants I must ask that the original contract be given back. If you take that away we will have no contract at all.
I merely wish to have a look at it in the morning.
You can see a copy of the contract any time you like.
What percentage on the total amount of the contract does the security represent?
Usually 10 per cent.

The security furnished here is $23,698 so that the tender would be for $236,698 and the time for completion is May, 1910. We are onlv asked to vote $150.000 of that amount, which leaves a balance of $86,000. The $150,000 we are now asked to vote is for the fiscal year 1910, which expires on the 31st of March, 1910. Therefore, this contractor is held to complete his work by the 1st of May, 1910, but he will have to expend some $86,950 in the moi 'n of April next. On the face of it your contract is an impossibility taken in connection with the present vote, unless you intend to extend the time for the completion of the contract.

We will have another session of parliament before the expiration of the contract. In April the canal is unwatered and he would do a large share of his work then. However, it is seldom that these contractors absolutely complete such contracts on time.
Is there a forfeit in this case?

I do not think there is a penalty in any of these cases, but they can only get an extension of time by order in council. Notwithstanding what has been said by my hon. friend who has hit the nail on the head fairly well, I may say that we do not want this year to expend any more money than we think is absolutely necessary.
Now we are getting at the reason.

Yes, my hon. friend struck the nail on the head as he quite often does-if the nail is in the right place. This year we believe not more than $150,000 can be expended, but if more is expended it can be provided for next year as we will have a session of parliament before the final estimate will be passed.

Then we are to understand that the government intends to add further to the depression throughout the Dominion by curtailing works that are necessary to be carried on in the interests of the country? We are going to have more men unfed and homes unprovided for owing to the fact that the government have brought a period of hard times on the country.
My hon. friend does not agree with some of his friends, the hon. member for North Toronto, for instance, that it is a time for economy.

HUGHES I am not speaking of economy. I am speaking of the conduct



oi public affairs. If the government wanted to be economical, they had plenty of opportunity during the years of plenty in the business of the country. This year and last year are lean years, and the government are in a panic and are hauling in their sails and turning on the labour market of the country thousands of unemployed men still further to increase the depression.
Does the hon. gentleman approve of the minister buying these 20.000 barrels of cement?

Not one barrel of that cement has been made since the minister gave the contract. It was old stock on hand. The cement men saw the depression coming, and they made a slick deal with the department in anticipation of it. Half of that cement will be useless when the works go on.

The hon. gentleman must remember that that cement had to be bought on account of all the permanent works being done at Montreal. Last year we made twenty miles of new streets, and we are going to make more next year. The minister had to buy the cement ahead to get it in time. The hon. gentleman says the government should give work. Well, the minister, by buying that cement, gave work to that factory.
Has the minister the information I asked for, as to the date when the tenders were received?
I have been unable to get it this evening; but I will bring it, with the names of all the tenderers, in the morning. In the meantime the item may stand.
Can the minister tell me whether the $40,000 worth of cement is now lying at the factory or at the canal?
It is in our storehouse in Montreal.

There is just one more element of danger which the minister's remarks bear, and it is this. He speaks of having given a definite contract of $238,000, and be now asks us to vote only $150,000, and he says that probably the contractors will go on and do more work than the appropriation will cover. Is that going to be the fixed policy of the government-to intimate to the contractors that we are having less money voted than we expect to spend this year, but that they can go on overexpending? 1 see in that an element of great danger. I hope the contractors will be given to understand that the government is responsible only for the moneys that parliament votes, and that until parliament votes a further sum they are taking a great risk in going beyond the amount voted.
Mr. sam. Hughes

We do that in the case of all contracts. We have notified all concerned that we want to keep the expenditure within the appropriations this year, and that if they go on and rush the work and over-run the amount voted, they do it at their own risk, because they cannot get any more cash until parliament votes it at another session.

The minister says that he does not see the object of bringing down the tenders except to show that the contract was let to the lowest tenderer. There is another reason why we desire to see the tenders. These tenders are sometimes made upon schedule prices. For instance, one tender may put rock excavation below another, and some other item, such as cement work, higher; and the engineer, in going over the various tenders, is able to tell the government which tender in the main is the lowest. It is interesting to see how he reaches his conclusion by comparing one tender with another. For that reason it is absolutely necessary to know what the schedule prices of various tenders are; otherwise one could not make an intelligent comparison. I understand that the hon. minister is satisfied to bring down all the tenders.

If my hon. friend wants them. There is not a man in the House who is not an engineer who can figure them out. We have an engineer in the department who ' moneys out ' these tend. rs. I will bring them down, though it has not been customary to do so.

I want to say, as one who has been in this House for a great many years, that it has been the custom.
Item allowed to stand.
Department of Public Printing and Stationery, $88,399.50.
Will the hon. minister explain that item?

The committee will observe that there is a difference of $36,824.50 between the total amount of these estimates for 1909-10 and the total amount of the same estimates for 1908-09. This difference is accounted for by an amount of $34,470.50, which represents the salaries paid to the employees brought under the Civil Service Act of last session and the remainder, namely, $2,354, represents the increases which have been granted the staff for the incoming year. The gentlemen who have been brought in from the outside, and whose salaries represent the greater amount of this increase, are as follows:	One in the
second division of subdivision A, who has been put in charge of what is called the franchise room. Then in the second division of subdivision B, two gentlemen have

been brought from the outside service. In former years these were paid out of the bulk sum voted for wages for the Printing Bureau, from what is known as the King's Printer's advance account .One of these occupied the position of chief foreman and the other of entry clerk. All these gentlemen were brought in at the salaries they were formerly receiving. There have been no new appointments, but simply a change in the status of the former employees, all of whom were in the outside service.
There is one new appointment.

There is a position there which has not been filled. In the third division, subdivision A, there have been eight clerks transferred. These gentlemen occupied various positions in the lithographic room, accountant's office, delivery office, and advertising and corresponding branch. Then there have been seventeen transferred to the third division, subdivision B. These are clerks now performing different duties in the stationery branch, accountant's branch, correspondent's branch, storekeeper's office and acting in secretarial positions. Then the last group representing the transfer of eleven from the outside to the inside service, is made up of the messengers and packers who were employed in the Bureau. The other positions, to which my hon. friend from Leeds referred, is that of Superintendent of Printing. The salaries are the same as these gentlemen formerly received plus the increases they are entitled to automatically.
Last year for the same service, there was only $75,000 required, and this year you require $81,000. Why this increase?
There have been no increases except the statutory increases under the new Act.
Will those amount to $6,000?
There is $1,000 in Deputy Minister's salary.
Yes, that is a statutory increase.

The total amount required for the outside service taken in is $31,000. The total amount expended last year for the inside service was $31,000. That makes $75,000 and you are asking $81,000, or an increase of nearly $6,000. How much would the statutory increases amount to? What increases were given the different officers, who are they, and why were they entitled to an increase?

I could best explain that by going over the list of the gentlemen brought in.
26J
Start with the Deputy Minister.
The Deputy Minister is Mr. C. H. Parmelee and he receives an increase of $1,000, which is a statutory increase.
Who is the first assistant to the King's Printer?
Mr. Wm. McMahon. Then in the first division, subdivision A, the gentleman whom my hon. friend from North Victoria inquired about was placed in that division.
I do not see any vote for 1908-9 for an assistant to the King's Printer?
That is a new title given Mr. McMahon, the Superintendent of 1 rinting, and he receives $2,900 per year.
1 understand that this Printing Bureau is paid for all the work it does for all the other departments at current rates?
That is my understanding.
Yet notwithstanding it shows a deficit of from $40,000 to $50,000. Why should it not be self-sustaining?
I do not challenge the statement, but shall inquire into it.

Printers throughout the country cannot understand why a bureau which receives contracts from all the other departments at fat prices should not be self sustaining. I am told that a lot of the work is duplicated. For instance, the work of setting up English is frequently given to French printers who are not very conversant with the language, and the setting of French work is given to English printers, who suffer under a like disability, and consequently the work of each has practically to be done over again. This has been brought to my attention by sev ral practical printers, who do not understand how this department needs a vote when it has good fat contracts for the printing of the several departments of the government.

I have not before heard the complaint to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. A. Currie) gives currency. I shall make inquiries, and, perhaps, at a later stage, I shall be able to inform the hon. gentleman and the committee definitely as to whether the statements made to the hon. gentleman have any foundation in fact. I may, however, point out that the Printing Bureau does a great deal of work outside of the departments Ur [DOT][DOT] hioh it is not paid-the issuing of 'Hansard', the printing of special reoorts, and a great many other things of that kind and these may possibly represent the amount to

which the hon. gentleman refers. As to the duplication of work of which the hon. gentleman has heard, I think that in all probability on inquiry it will turn out to be in large measure unfounded.
What becomes every year of the money we vote for ' Hansard '.
It is true there is a vote for * Hansard '.

Then, why try to give the impression that this item is virtually to pay for 'Hansard'? If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Murphy) will ascertain from the foreman of his printing department how much money was expended for straight setting and how much for corrections, he will soon ascertain whether I am correct or not. And I will ask him to bring that information down before we pass the item. For there is not a newspaper man in Canada who is not interested in this matter, especially those who run job offices. They would like to have a share of the government's business, and cannot see why the government maintain a bureau at great expense to do work that might as well be done outside.

I do not know that I clearly understand the explanation the hon. minister tries to make. The amount voted for 1908-1909 was $44,475. The amount asked for next year is $81,299.50. The hon. minister says that he is paying out of this vote amounts which formerly were paid out of outside votes and that he is paying the exact amount of salaries that those taken in from outside had on September 1 last. The foot-note shows that the votes for those in the outside service for 1908-1909 was $28,722.83, with increases under the Act from September 1 1908, to March 31, 1909, of $1,154.78. The statutory increases only amount to $1,200. So, we have a deficiency still to be accounted for something like $6,000, of which $1,200 is taken up as the minister says.
No, $2,354, as appears in the estimates.
Does that include the $150 proposed to be added to the salary of each civil servant?
No, nor does it include $1,000 increase to the deputy minister under the Act of last year.
Then, there is still $3,000 left.
Speaking subject to correction as to the exact figures, my understanding is that whatever difference there may be is represented by increases to these gentlemen brought in.

Will the hon. minister kindly point out to me in the Audi-Mr. MURPHY.
tor General's Report the details of expenditure for last year in this department?
I have not the report at hand.
I have two volumes 4 of it here.
Unless they appear in those volumes-
They do not, and that is one reason why I think the item should be allowed to stand.

Will the minister give us the name of the officer for whom this $2,900 is provided, and tell us whether he was in the service before or not? If he was in the service, from what position did he retire and what salary was he receiving?
If he was not in the service, what special qualification had he that he was given this prominent position over the heads of others?

The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart) has asked me with regard to the position for which the amount of $2,125 is provided. That is for the unfilled position of Superintendent of Printing. Until I am satisfied that some person is required in that position, there will be no appointment. The position was held by Mr. McMahon until last month, when he was promoted to be assistant King's Printer, his salary being represented by the item of $2,900. He has been in the Bureau since its organization, and was in the employ of the contractors for government printing before that. He has special qualifications for the office. He received a salary of $2,800, and this additional $100 represent the statutory increase.
Of what department is the deputy minister here referred to a deputy?

My knowledge of that is confined to what I have learned from the statute. The law creating the Department of Public Printing and Stationery provides that it shall be attached to the Department of the Secretary of State, who is given administration of the department.
Heretofore there has been no deputy?
Yes, the former deputy was Dr. Dawson, who was superannuated on account of failing health and age.
But $1,000 was added for the new man, who, it happens, was a member of this House.
That $1,000 was added by the statute of last session which fixed the salaries of certain deputies at $5,000.
Has any application been received for the unfilled position?
A great many, but each applicant has received the stock answer that the minister in charge is not satisfied that it is necessary to make any appointment.
The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) is a practical printer, and if the Secretary of State will apply to him he will recommend him a good man.
There will be a reduction in the outside service vote to correspond with the increase in this?
Yes.
What is the amount of the reduction?

I have not the particulars, but when the item is reached I will have the information.
Fumigation stations, $5,000.

I have been doing this work for some years, and it is going on satisfactorily. There is one station at St. John, N.B., one at St. Johns, Que., one on the Niagara frontier, at Beechburg, I think, one at Windsor, one at Winnipeg and one at Vancouver.
For the enforcement of the 'Gold and Silver Marking Act, 1908,' $4,000.

This is a new item. Last year we passed an Act providing for certain markings on gold and silver ornaments or plate, which are being sold, and we have been appealed to by the trade to appoint an inspector to enforce the Act. I thought at one time there would be no necessity for an inspector, but I have been informed that the Act is being violated, and the trade has appealed to us strongly to enforce it.
Who is the officer?
He has not yet been appointed.
I understand you are providing $4,000' for an officer. How do you provide for his travelling expenses?
And expenses for prosecution, if there are any. We hope that the $4,000 will cover everything. I have not fixed the salary yet.
What will be the qualifications?

I hope to get some one who is acquainted with the gold and silver trade.
Tracadie and D'Arey Island Lazarettos, and leprosy generally, $10,000.

There is an increase of $2,000 due to the fact that we have been trying to deport Chinese lepers in British Columbia. As a rule these men are quite
willing to be deported and sent back to China, and the authorities there have no objection to their being landed in China. Unfortunately, we are finding more of this class than we had expected, and we shall probably require a larger sum.
Would not that properly come under the immigration expenditure?

It has been managed by us, because we have control of the leprosy-stations at Tracadie and D'Arey island. Some of these people have been in British Columbia for years and could not be deported by the immigration authorities.
Then if the time has passed which allows their being deported under the Immigration Act, what authority b/ive you for deporting them under any other Act?

No authority except their being willing to go, we paying the expenses to send them.
Public Works Health Act, $8,000.
Is that for the purpose of paying inspectors of public works to see whether the general precautions regarding health are being carried out?
Yes.
How many are employed for that work, and how are they engaged- by the year?

They are engaged by the year and they travel about and examine public works wherever they are being constructed. I had only one until about fifteen or eighteen months ago when I found the work was very heavy and increasing, especially in the west, and I had to appoint another. That gentleman resigned a couple of months ago and I have not yet appointed a successor,
What salary do you pay?

Either $1,500 or $1,800 a
year and travelling expenses.
Who is the man who resigned?
Dr. Chamberlain. He was working in the west.
Does the inspector from time to time visit the works or does he only make one inspection during the season?
He must visit them once in three months.

Who is the inspector
now?
Mr. Fisher. He has been the inspector since the commencement of the work.
Has any person taken Dr. Chamberlain's position?
Not yet. I expect to appoint some one. During the winter there is not such a large amount of work going on.
It is about a year since Dr. Chamberlain resigned?
No, not later than last summer.
I think it was about June.
I think it was later than June, but I am not positive.
Suppose the inspector finds the conditions unsatisfactory, what is done?	'

The contractor is notified and if he does not immediately comply with the law he may be prosecuted. I do not remember that we have had any case of prosecution. The moment complaint is made the inspector is ordered to go, even if he has been there a month ago, to examine into the facts of the case and make a report.
Do I understand that there have been complaints?

Yes. In one case where the complaints were partially well founded the contractors were notified that they must remedy the grievance. The Act and the rgulations specify what provision must be made for he employees and what precautions must be taken. The rule is that contractors are allowed to take a small sum, I think fifty cents a month, from the wages of the employees to cover the expenses.
Is that duty imposed upon the contractor by reason of his contract or by reason of the Public Health Act?
By reason of the Public Health Act.
There is no clause in the contract in regard to that?
Not necessarily. There might or might not be.
For what purpose is that fifty cents a month taken from the employees?
For the purpose of giving them medical attendance.
That is a different thing altogether from the inspection of public works.

It has nothing to do with the pay of our inspector. It reimburses the contractors for the outlay they are obliged to- make in the interest of their em-Mr. FISHER.
ployees in providing hospitals and medical attendance. It is very much in the nature of an assessment in a union or organization of any kind for the purpose of insuring the members of that organization medical attendance.
That has been the common practice for thirty years?

Yes, and that Act simply provides that certain requirements shall be complied with in consequence of holding back that amount of money.
Pensions-Mrs. Delaney, $400.
That is for Mrs. Delaney, whose husband was shot at Frog lake?
I think it is.

I support the item very strongly, but I want to draw the attention of the government to the fact that the men who, while defending their country, were shot down at Frog lake have never had their graves decorated or cared for in any way. 1 brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) last year and I would be pleased if the Minister of Customs, who is leading the House to-night, would take it into his serious consideration and have the graves of the late Messrs. Delaney, Gowanlock and Gilchrist looked after. I beg to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) to it. These graves should be put within a little railing. It would not cost much; it would be a matter of courtesy, and I am sure that the soldiers throughout the country would appreciate it very much.

I will make inquiry about it.
Pensions payable on account of the Fenian Raid, $2,000.

I noticed the other day that when the veterans were before the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia and Defence it was said by some of them that there had been no recognition of the services of those who had served in defence of their country upon the occasion of this raid other than those who received wounds and were disabled. There was a certain recognition.
Hon! Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia). There was not only a recognition of those who were wounded, but if my hon. friend had been present at that meeting he would have seen that there was a recognition of the services of every man who turned out in defence of the country at that time, because he would have seen the evidence of it on the left breast of each man in the medal which he wore and which is the very highest recognition that can possibly be given by any country.
Last year a pension was granted to the widow and children of the late Lt.-Col. Hallowell who was wounded at Batoche and died last year. Is that a pension that would require a vote?

No, that is statutory under the Militia Pension Act.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. PATERSON moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?
It is private members' day, but if we reach government orders we will go into Supply.
What department?

I cannot say.
